That the first report of the standing committee on external affairs, presented on February 12, 1959, be now concurred in.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
subsubtopic: MOTION FOR CONCURRENCE IN FIRST REPORT OF STANDING COMMITTEE
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I understood yesterday from the leader of the house that he was going to make a motion dealing with other matters. I would like to address myself to the motion and perhaps discuss it at the same time, if I am allowed to.

subsubtopic: MOTION FOR CONCURRENCE IN FIRST REPORT OF STANDING COMMITTEE

subsubtopic: MOTION FOR CONCURRENCE IN FIRST REPORT OF STANDING COMMITTEE
speechtext: May I be allowed to present the position of the opposition with respect to the matter that is now before the house?

subsubtopic: MOTION FOR CONCURRENCE IN FIRST REPORT OF STANDING COMMITTEE
speechtext:
I will hear the hon. member after I put the motion. It has been moved by Mr. Dinsdale for Mr. White, seconded by Mr. Hamilton (York West), by unanimous consent:
That the first report of the standing committee on external affairs presented on February 12, 1959, be now concurred in.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
subsubtopic: MOTION FOR CONCURRENCE IN FIRST REPORT OF STANDING COMMITTEE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I thank the hon. member for Middlesex East for allowing this motion to stand over until today. What I intend to say now is that this motion, if it is passed, will create a serious hardship for those of us who sit in the opposition on this side of the house. I refer particularly to that part of the report which seeks the authority of the house to sit while the house is sitting.
There are many things I could say on the subject matter in general, but I know it is not the intention to have a general debate on it and I shall be brief. I shall say this
only. If the government wished it could, as it did at one period last year, have a number of those committees sitting at the same time. For instance, I am informed that at one stage last year there were as many as six committees sitting while the house was sitting. On the six committees which reported yesterday there are 66 members from the Liberal side of the house. That in effect means this, that if all of us were to attend to our duties in the committees there would be no one, or practically no one, left in the house to look after the business of the house. That is why I say this is taking undue advantage of the position in which the opposition finds itself. I should also like to point out to the government that this is the first time in the last 20 or 25 years at least that the opposition has found itself in such a position.

subsubtopic: MOTION FOR CONCURRENCE IN FIRST REPORT OF STANDING COMMITTEE
speechtext: Oh, no.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
subsubtopic: MOTION FOR CONCURRENCE IN FIRST REPORT OF STANDING COMMITTEE
speechtext: Well, let me give the figures and we will see. I am informed that from 1936 to 1940 there were 74 members in the opposition, from 1940 to 1945 there were 67, from 1949 to 1953 there were 75 and from 1953 to 1957 there were 95.

subsubtopic: MOTION FOR CONCURRENCE IN FIRST REPORT OF STANDING COMMITTEE
speechtext: You mean in all parties.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
subsubtopic: MOTION FOR CONCURRENCE IN FIRST REPORT OF STANDING COMMITTEE
speechtext:
All parties. Today in all parties there are 57, I believe, which is a considerably smaller number than obtained in those years. The result is that we are being asked to do now a far greater amount of work than was required at that time, and I think it is unfortunate that the government is giving no consideration to that position.
May I remind the house that the Prime Minister on more than one occasion-I think at least twice-gave some indication to the house that he intended to come to the assistance of those of us who sit in the opposition by providing us with additional help of some kind. That was not forthcoming, and I am not complaining; but what I am complaining about is that we who sit on this side of the house are not in a position to fulfil adequately the three responsibilities we have to fulfil, namely to sit as members of these committees while the house is sitting if the government so decides, to attend to office work involving correspondence and the like which must of necessity be handled in the forenoon, and to sit in the house to attend to our parliamentary duties.

External Affairs Committee
So I ask the government to give consideration to the position in which we find ourselves. It is a condition that perhaps I should not be complaining unduly about from the point of view of representation, but I am complaining about it from the point of view of work. This is simply asking too much of us. I believe I know what the house leader is going to say. He is going to say that they are taking this power now and may not use it, or may not use it until near the end of the session. My reply is that the power should not be taken unless it is intended to use it. It is quite easy for a committee to take this power in the dying days of the session when it is perhaps necessary to do so, but I do want to insist on the fact that if the government desires to have four or five or six committees sit and we have to attend to our duties on those committees, it will be next to impossible to attend to those duties and be in the house at the same time. I ask the government if it will not reconsider the untenable position in which we are placed at the moment.

speakeroldname: Hon. Howard C. Green (Minister of Public Works):

subsubtopic: MOTION FOR CONCURRENCE IN FIRST REPORT OF STANDING COMMITTEE
speechtext: I know that while we were in opposition, although we got along splendidly with our friends of the C.C.F. and Social Credit parties we certainly were never in the position in which the Liberals find themselves today, of trying to take the C.C.F. in and make one party.

subsubtopic: MOTION FOR CONCURRENCE IN FIRST REPORT OF STANDING COMMITTEE

subsubtopic: MOTION FOR CONCURRENCE IN FIRST REPORT OF STANDING COMMITTEE

subsubtopic: MOTION FOR CONCURRENCE IN FIRST REPORT OF STANDING COMMITTEE

subsubtopic: MOTION FOR CONCURRENCE IN FIRST REPORT OF STANDING COMMITTEE

I submit that this is very material, because the hon. member for Laurier argued that there were only 57 members to do all the work of the opposition. He treated them as one big lump. Surely I am in order in talking in this vein. I am very serious about what I say. This C.C.F. party, throughout its history in the House of Commons, has stood on its own feet and not tried to combine with any other party. Sometimes it will support one party or the other, and the next day it will be against them. I am sure that is their position today.
This attempt, just for the purpose of making an argument, to lump the C.C.F. with the Liberal party in a request that they not be made to work too hard and to try to get sympathy, is just a lot of poppycock. The actual fact is that these Liberals do not want to work too hard, and they are never here to work in the first place. Here you have eight members of the C.C.F. taking their full part in the debates in the house, and going into a committee where they may have only half a member-

subsubtopic: MOTION FOR CONCURRENCE IN FIRST REPORT OF STANDING COMMITTEE
speechtext: Oh, oh.

subsubtopic: MOTION FOR CONCURRENCE IN FIRST REPORT OF STANDING COMMITTEE
speechtext:
-yet that half member makes more noise than all the rest of the committee put together.
Now, the sad and harrowing tale we are told today, that the poor Liberals are so tired they cannot possibly do their duty in the committees, is just too bad. What was our position when we were in opposition? For 18 long years we had fewer members than there are in the Liberal opposition today. It may be that from 1953 to 1957 we had about the same number as there are in the official opposition today.

subsubtopic: MOTION FOR CONCURRENCE IN FIRST REPORT OF STANDING COMMITTEE
speechtext: What about from 1945 to 1949?

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
subsubtopic: MOTION FOR CONCURRENCE IN FIRST REPORT OF STANDING COMMITTEE
speechtext: For the whole time, except from 1945 to 1949, we were in the same position or a worse position than they are today. Did we come whimpering to the house?

subsubtopic: MOTION FOR CONCURRENCE IN FIRST REPORT OF STANDING COMMITTEE
speechtext: You certainly did.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
subsubtopic: MOTION FOR CONCURRENCE IN FIRST REPORT OF STANDING COMMITTEE
speechtext: We used the small numbers we had, and three or four men on the front benches did not try to do all the work. This is one of the reasons that we are over here on the government side today. Today the Leader of the Opposition is just like the little boy at the dike, only he is running from one dike to the other all the time the house is sitting trying to stop all the holes.

subsubtopic: MOTION FOR CONCURRENCE IN FIRST REPORT OF STANDING COMMITTEE
speechtext: The water is certainly coming through.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
subsubtopic: MOTION FOR CONCURRENCE IN FIRST REPORT OF STANDING COMMITTEE
speechtext: The government is going in all directions.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
subsubtopic: MOTION FOR CONCURRENCE IN FIRST REPORT OF STANDING COMMITTEE
speechtext:
These Liberals were in power so long, sitting in their seats and letting other people do the work, that they do not know how to take their coats off and get to work. They have able men on the back benches. For example, there is the hon. member for Nipissing. Why not let him lead one of their teams in the committees? What is the position, Mr. Speaker? The motion, in its present terms, has been the customary motion for many years.

subsubtopic: MOTION FOR CONCURRENCE IN FIRST REPORT OF STANDING COMMITTEE

subsubtopic: MOTION FOR CONCURRENCE IN FIRST REPORT OF STANDING COMMITTEE

subsubtopic: MOTION FOR CONCURRENCE IN FIRST REPORT OF STANDING COMMITTEE
speechtext: Ever since I came here in 1935. The hon. member for Essex East I understand agreed in the committee on external affairs that this report was the correct report.

subsubtopic: MOTION FOR CONCURRENCE IN FIRST REPORT OF STANDING COMMITTEE
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I rise on a point of order. I said no such thing. What I said to the chairman was that we would agree to it on the understanding that it would not interfere with our obligations in this house; and that is the tenor of the submission made by the hon. member for Laurier (Mr. Chevrier) and now being ignored by my genial friend the master of irrelevancy.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
subsubtopic: MOTION FOR CONCURRENCE IN FIRST REPORT OF STANDING COMMITTEE
speechtext: I must admit, Mr. Speaker, that the hon. member for Essex East should be a good judge of irrelevancy.

subsubtopic: MOTION FOR CONCURRENCE IN FIRST REPORT OF STANDING COMMITTEE

subsubtopic: MOTION FOR CONCURRENCE IN FIRST REPORT OF STANDING COMMITTEE
speechtext: Let us consider, for example, this motion in connection with the report of the external affairs committee which is under consideration. This committee will be hearing General McNaughton one of these days. General McNaughton has many other things to do. He is out of the country a good deal. It has been the custom to hear him right through when he is called. Perhaps only as a matter of courtesy he will be heard in the afternoon when the house is sitting. It is perfectly proper that this committee should ask for that power. I do not think my hon. friends can bring out one instance in the last session when they were not given reasonable treatment in every committee of the house.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
subsubtopic: MOTION FOR CONCURRENCE IN FIRST REPORT OF STANDING COMMITTEE
speechtext:
Yes, I can give an example. While the committee on public accounts was sitting we were asked to sit both morning and afternoon while the house was sitting, and we
External Affairs Committee protested. Not only did we protest but we said that we would not attend the meetings of the committee, because we felt that the business of the house was more important than that of the committee. That is what I am pointing to.

subsubtopic: MOTION FOR CONCURRENCE IN FIRST REPORT OF STANDING COMMITTEE
speechtext: Oh, oh.

subsubtopic: MOTION FOR CONCURRENCE IN FIRST REPORT OF STANDING COMMITTEE

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
subsubtopic: MOTION FOR CONCURRENCE IN FIRST REPORT OF STANDING COMMITTEE

That statement applies, of
course, not only to our side of the house but also to the hon. member for Laurier in so far as he took part in the deliberations of the committee, and to the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate (Mr. Pickersgill). subsubtopic: MOTION FOR CONCURRENCE IN FIRST REPORT OF STANDING COMMITTEE

subsubtopic: MOTION FOR CONCURRENCE IN FIRST REPORT OF STANDING COMMITTEE

subsubtopic: MOTION FOR CONCURRENCE IN FIRST REPORT OF STANDING COMMITTEE
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I do not think the serious business of the House of Commons deserves the type of speech to which we have just been subjected.

I think it is most inappropriate for the leader of the government in the house to take this attitude toward this important business that comes before us. It seems to me

External Affairs Committee that it is a growing attitude on the part of this government, and that the government does not consider seriously the things that are being discussed. Instead of giving us some sound argument, and instead of trying to co-operate with all members of the house in dealing with the business of the house, we are subjected to a type of soapbox oratory which only the Minister of Public Works can attain.

subsubtopic: MOTION FOR CONCURRENCE IN FIRST REPORT OF STANDING COMMITTEE
speechtext: Oh, oh.

subsubtopic: MOTION FOR CONCURRENCE IN FIRST REPORT OF STANDING COMMITTEE
speechtext:
I am not at all offended by the things he said about the Liberals and the C.C.F. party. I know that when the Liberals were on the government benches we had a couple of Tory parties in this house, and now that the Liberals are in opposition they can, of course, change their attitude in certain ways. But we have demonstrated at all times that we are prepared to take a clear stand on our own. I think a vote which demonstrated this most aptly this session was a vote which might not have been necessary except that the government thought it might put the opposition on the spot by calling a vote on the main motion with regard to the address in reply to the speech from the throne. But on that occasion we found these two old Tory parties, one calling itself Liberal and the other Progressive Conservative, in the same bag voting together.
Mr. Speaker, it is impossible for members of this house to act effectively on committees when the government follows the policy of having a great many committees meet while the house is sitting. There is no member of this house who does not wish to expedite the work of the house and the work of the committees; but this is a method, from the experience we had last session, which the government is using to make it virtually impossible for members of parliament to carry on in an effective way the business that is their responsibility.
We have heard about important people coming to appear before committees, and the difficulty of keeping them here for a number of days if the committees do not sit when the house is sitting. There is something in that argument, but only something. I do not know of any instance in the past when opposition members have objected to necessary sittings in order to hear important witnesses. In years gone by I can remember when we have had important witnesses appearing before the agriculture committee, such as members of the board of grain commissioners, members of the wheat board, some of the veterinarians concerning the great controversy over foot-and-mouth disease, but we always got the same story: "We have to


have extra sittings because these people have to get back to Winnipeg". We have had the extra sittings, have missed work in the house, and some of these important witnesses have been seen walking around the corridors for another day.
Therefore I think the members of this house should not support this measure at this time, a measure designed by the government to make it impossible for members of the opposition to do the kind of work that is their responsibility. How often have we heard the Prime Minister when in opposition say to the government that they should not use their big majority to override the opposition in such a way as to undermine the effectiveness of the House of Commons. I suggest that at this time, when this session is barely under way, this is no day to ask for the blanket approval of one motion after another to give all these committees the right to sit when the house is sitting.

speakeroldname: Hon. L. B. Pearson (Leader of ihe Opposiiion):
subsubtopic: MOTION FOR CONCURRENCE IN FIRST REPORT OF STANDING COMMITTEE
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, perhaps it would not have been necessary for me to take part in this discussion if it had not been for the amusing but meaningless irrelevancies of my hon. friend the leader of the house, who tried to tell us on this side, with that amiable arrogance which at times is characteristic of him, how we should do our job. We appreciate his advice-

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
subsubtopic: MOTION FOR CONCURRENCE IN FIRST REPORT OF STANDING COMMITTEE
speechtext: If you followed it.

subsubtopic: MOTION FOR CONCURRENCE IN FIRST REPORT OF STANDING COMMITTEE
speechtext:
If we followed it we would probably be following very bad advice indeed; because surely, Mr. Speaker, it is not really the objective of the leader of the house to help us do our job. He might well lure us into a position where he would not be able to do it as effectively as otherwise we would. Therefore his advice is suspect on this matter, as is also his impassioned defence of the rights of the C.C.F. against the effort on our part, Mr. Speaker, to link ourselves with the C.C.F., as we shall do on all matters which affect the rights of the opposition in this house.
We remember, Mr. Speaker, the emotional and impassioned utterances of the present Prime Minister about the rights of the opposition against what he used to call an arrogant majority trying to dictate and determine how business in this house should be conducted. We remember even in the last session the assurance he gave us that not only would everything be done that could be done to give the opposition their rights in this house, but that no step would be taken to prevent the opposition discharging its primary duty, which is in the House of Commons and not primarily in committees.

We object to this move on the part of the government to divert-and it is more than a 15 per cent diversion-more and more of the business of this house to committees at the beginning of the session in accordance with the United States style of congressional government, which inevitably will prevent the opposition from doing its main job in the House of Commons where the work of government should be primarily conducted.
The minister said this kind of motion has been made for 20 or 25 years. I would ask him to point to any motion in 25 years which at the very beginning of the session, shortly after the debate on the speech from the throne concluded, sought to set up so many committees or give so many of them the right to sit while the house is in session. It has been done in respect of isolated committees on rare occasions, but we are being asked to agree to this step with respect to six committees. I suggest it is unprecedented, and if it is not unprecedented it is surely highly irregular.
We in the opposition are not alone in objecting to this motion. In the agriculture committee yesterday when this question came up, 10 of the Conservative members of that committee voted against the proposal to give the committee this power. I am quite sure that these 10 hon. gentlemen, being independent Conservative members, will undoubtedly support the stand we are taking on their behalf as well as on our own behalf at this time.
We base our case on the fact that it is reasonable. We are not whining or asking for sympathy. I believe we will be able to do our job without the help of the leader of the house. We are simply asking that this matter be postponed until it becomes clear that it is necessary for these committees to sit while the house is in session. Surely that is a reasonable position. When the time comes, as it undoubtedly will, when these committees have to sit while the house is in session we will co-operate in any motion to that effect; but to ask us to do so at the beginning of the session is unnecessary and unwarranted.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. J. G. Diefenbaker (Prime Minister):
subsubtopic: MOTION FOR CONCURRENCE IN FIRST REPORT OF STANDING COMMITTEE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am not going to enter into the apparent controversy between the two groups in the opposition, except to note that the hon. member for Assiniboia (Mr. Argue) certainly disavowed at the earliest possible opportunity the marriage of inconvenience that was suggested by the hon. member for Laurier (Mr. Chevrier). He was not taking any chances on that, and he made it very clear.
I for one am always most anxious to see
that the house operates in a way that allows
External Affairs Committee the opposition to place its views properly and fairly before the house. I know something of what it is to be a member of a small opposition, and I realize that the responsibilities resting upon an opposition are very great. When an opposition endeavours to place before the house and the country its ideas and suggestions, that is after all its duty, objective, purpose and responsibility.
The Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Pearson) speaks about this horrible innovation of having committees sit while the house is sitting and tells what a shock it has been to him that we should ever suggest that committees sit while the house is sitting, but I would point out to him that I have before me the Journals of 1956. I find recorded there that the house opened on January 11 in that year. The committee on banking and commerce presented its first report on March 6 and requested that the quorum be reduced and that permission be granted to sit while the house was sitting, to which unanimous concurrence was given. On March 8 there was a further motion that the committee on public accounts be given permission to sit while the house was sitting, and by unanimous consent the report was concurred in. On March 13 the standing committee on external affairs presented its first report and recommended that it be authorized to sit while the house was sitting, and again by unanimous consent the report was concurred in.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
subsubtopic: MOTION FOR CONCURRENCE IN FIRST REPORT OF STANDING COMMITTEE
speechtext: May I ask the Prime Minister a question?

subsubtopic: MOTION FOR CONCURRENCE IN FIRST REPORT OF STANDING COMMITTEE
speechtext: Surely.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
subsubtopic: MOTION FOR CONCURRENCE IN FIRST REPORT OF STANDING COMMITTEE
speechtext: Was there any occasion in Votes and Proceedings or Journals from which the hon. member is reading when six committees asked for this power in February?

subsubtopic: MOTION FOR CONCURRENCE IN FIRST REPORT OF STANDING COMMITTEE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, all that is being done at the moment is that the committees are being set up and given this power. This is an act on the part of this house to give this power at this time, and I shall make it very clear that whenever the hon. members of this house fairly and responsibly find themselves in a position in which an injustice is being done in any way and the matter is brought to my attention, I shall do everything I can to rectify it.
All we are asking is that power be given to these committees to sit while the house is sitting, as has been done in the past and as has been recommended in the first report of committees on previous occasions. Certainly there is nothing out of the ordinary in such a move. The position taken by those in opposition is purely a smokescreen designed to lead the Canadian people to think that because we
990	HOUSE OF
External Affairs Committee have a majority we on this side of the house are trying to use it unfairly over the opposition. We have done everything to ensure that every opportunity will be given to the opposition to discharge its responsibilities in a proper manner. I for one will say unequivocally that if at any time there is any action taken that would deny members of the opposition a fair opportunity of discharging their responsibility, I shall immediately see to it that a change is made in order to assure justice and fairness.
All this talk this morning is simply designed to create the impression that we are seeking to prevent discussion. I only hope that hon. gentlemen opposite continue to discuss this question in the manner they have, because having regard to some of the contributions made and as long as the discussion is of the nature of that which has occurred here today -a nature that has characterized their contributions in this house on more than one occasion-there will be nothing in particular to be concerned about on our part.

subsubtopic: MOTION FOR CONCURRENCE IN FIRST REPORT OF STANDING COMMITTEE

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, while I like to have a kindly man advising me at all times, I think it is hardly in keeping with the traditions of this House of Commons that one man should rise in his place and advise his little family that they can rest assured; father knows best, and if at any time there may be any little bit of hardship or any little bit of inconvenience or difficulty, they can all come running back to father and papa will look after their needs and assure them that they will be well looked after. I think that attitude, Mr. Speaker, is most disrespectful of the functions this House of Commons ought to perform.
After all, if these committees will not be needing this power for some time yet I see no reason why the age-old practice, which is well established by precedents, should not be adhered to. If and when the time arrives that these committees must meet


while the house is sitting, a separate motion can then be brought before the house. This has happened over and over again, except in the odd instance. However, exceptions are not the rule, even though in the opinion of some they may make the rule.
Who decides whether committees of this house shall sit while the house is sitting? I maintain it should be the members of this House of Commons, and not any one individual. We used to complain about parliament being run by the cabinet. I believe, Mr. Speaker, a dangerous situation is now arising because we now have not only parliament but the cabinet being ruled by one single individual. The members of the House of Commons are supposed to rest content; they are supposed to waive their rights and prerogatives in favour of a blanket assurance that all their wishes are going to be respected. I am realistic enough to know that kind father cannot keep those promises, because no parliament would be able to function efficiently if the members were always assured that all the wishes and conveniences of individual members were going to be attended to.
No, Mr. Speaker; after listening to a television broadcast the other evening I fully realized that there were many members in this House of Commons who may be-and for various reasons-unable to participate as effectively as they might like to in the work of the House of Commons, and that therefore there may be political hay to be made outside the House of Commons by making newspaper headlines through the speeches they make somewhere outside this house.
I have many reasons to believe that one of the urgent reasons for this motion is to give some of the backbench supporters of this government a chance to make a little bit of political hay which they otherwise would be unable to make. I hear there are many independent Conservatives who agree that there is no need for this motion, and I would like to move, seconded by the hon. member for Timmins (Mr. Martin) that the motion now before us be amended by deleting therefrom recommendation No. 1 and renumbering the present recommendation No. 2 as No. 1.

Mr. Speaker, I move, seconded by the hon. member for Skeena (Mr. Howard), that this report be referred back to the committee.
Surely the Prime Minister does not expect the members of the opposition to have the same confidence in his assurances that he has himself or that the members of his party may have. Yesterday we attended three of those committee meetings, and we were surprised at several aspects of those meetings. I assumed that these were meetings of the members of the committees as they were brought in by the striking committee. I assumed that the members were going to decide on the things that were to take place in those committees, but that is just not true. In one particular instance, when the clerk of the committee asked for nominations I moved a nomination and the nomination was completely ignored, although there was a seconder available. The committee went on to accept the motion that had been prepared previously on a party basis, and that is what was expected. The parliamentary procedure that normally prevails in a committee, as it is understood on this side of the house, was not observed in this instance.
As I understand the procedure, the clerk calls for the nomination. An hon. member moves the nomination, and as a rule in committee it does not need to be seconded. The nominee has not the right to withdraw until the nominations are closed. He can then choose to withdraw or accept the nomination. Those elementary rules were not followed. Several other motions were moved. Those motions were moved and the names of those who were moving and seconding them were written down on a piece of paper. These names were not proposed by the committee but came from some other source as a matter of policy. I suggest that this is not my understanding of how committees should be constituted and how their work should be carried out.
I was also very surprised to learn that a motion such as this should be introduced at this time in the three committees that I attended. After all, it was only the first day that the committees sat. This is no longer an emergency session. This is not a session that was called with an election anticipated very shortly.

speechtext:
What I should like to bring to the attention of the house leader and the government is this. It was my experience during the sittings of committees last year that this practice has not worked out satisfactorily. I had hoped that the government would not see fit to refer these estimates of various departments to separate committees, save and except, to the committee on estimates which was established for that purpose; the reason being that my experience in the committee on railways, canals and telegraph lines dealing with the Department of Transport estimates was such that I thought-and I am sure it was the thought of most of the members who were there-that it was a complete waste of time to have the departmental officials go before the committee, particularly in a department like the Department of Transport which is so huge and takes in so many branches of transportation and communications, and for the committee to take up the time of those officials with a repetition of matters that would unquestionably come up for discussion again in the house on the estimates in general.
9S4

National Revenue
It had seemed to us that perhaps that practice could have been stopped this year. I am happy to say that one thing the government has decided to do is discontinue the practice of study groups; because that, as the house saw last year, was a complete loss of time. While it might have been of assistance to certain members on the other side of the house, there are ways and means of assisting new members, and it seemed to me that that should not be done at the expense of those of us who are so few in number on this side.
There was one other point, if I may be permitted to make it, and I shall do my best not to trespass on the time of the house. These committees will be sitting in the morning, and as the house leader knows there are 17 standing committees to which will be added the special committees, so I think they may run to as many as 20 or more. Those committees may sit during the morning; and if the estimates are sent to these various committees then it becomes impossible to carry on the work of the house. It becomes impossible to carry on the work which has to be done in each office and to prepare for the work of the house during the course of the afternoon or the morning, according to the time the house sits.
Therefore I appeal to the house leader and to the government and ask them if it would not be much better to allow these estimates to go to the estimates committee rather than send them to the separate committees requiring the attendance of members of the house. I ask that with all respect, because it seems to me to be a duplication of our work. I realize that the government has its difficulties, and we had the same difficulties when we were on that side of the house, with reference to the large number of new members and so forth; but as I said earlier, there are ways and means of dealing with that situation.
The Prime Minister, in speaking to one of these motions last year, indicated the manner in which that could be done. He also indicated that perhaps some assistance could be given, but there was no sequel to that indication. The Prime Minister further indicated that he hoped that one of these committees would deal with certain matters in the same way the war expenditures committee had dealt with them when he and I had the privilege of sitting on such a committee at one time.
I do not want to get into an argument, because I have received unanimous consent to speak, but unfortunately that committee did not operate in the method and in the manner expected by the Prime Minister. The Prime Minister says now, "Well, if there is any difficulty, come to me and I will see that

it is straightened out." It seems to me that while that is a nice gesture on the part of the Prime Minister, that is not the way in which the business of the house should be conducted; and I appeal, with deference, to the house leader and the government that these estimates in particular should not go to separate committees so the whole business will have to be repeated when the estimates are before the house.

Our main purpose in adopting this system last year was to try to work out a more efficient method of dealing with the estimates. Mind you, we were also attracted to this course by the desire to allow new members of the house to obtain quickly an understanding of the way business is done; and I think, by and large, the work done by the various committees which dealt with estimates last year was good.
We are not trying to deceive the opposition parties in taking this position. We are simply trying to work out a more efficient way of handling the business of the house, and in this connection we have had very good co-operation from the hon. member for Laurier and the hon. member for Assiniboia (Mr. Argue). speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in view of the intense interest by news sources in the last few days in the search for oil in the Arctic islands, I thought I owed it to the house to make a statement as to what is actually transpiring.
Since the middle of January, 1959 there have been 10 oil companies and individuals who have made application for oil and gas lands in the northern islands of Canada and on lands underlying the coastal waters bordering Canada. I should like to emphasize to the house that this is in addition to the 76 million acres now under permit in the mainland of the Northwest Territories and the Yukon.
In the Arctic islands the oil and gas regulations are being revised, and until such time as the revision is complete no permits are being issued. However, applications are being received and filed on a priority of application basis so that when the revised regulations come into effect, those who have made application, upon payment of the required deposits and fees, will be issued permits to explore for oil and gas in accordance with the priority list.

Inquiries of the Ministry
Up to 11 a.m. this morning approximately 50 million acres had been applied for in the Arctic archipelago covering geological structures and gypsum domes, extending from Banks island on the southwest and easterly to the northerly portion of Baffin island, north to the north-central part of Ellesmere island and southwesterly through the Sverdrup islands to Banks island. The geological survey of Canada have completed a study of this area, and are presently preparing a full report on the Queen Elizabeth islands. It is expected that the westerly portion will be available for distribution by March 1, 1959.
I have here a list of the companies and the acreage taken out, but I shall reserve that for a later announcement, probably in committee.
Along the west coast of Canada, Pdchfield Corporation have applied for acreage underlying the waters in the vicinity of Graham island in British Columbia, and Canadian Homestead Oils Limited have applied for acreage under the Fraser river delta. There is approximately 500,000 acres in the two areas applied for by these companies. Underlying the waters of Hudson bay and James bay, along the southwesterly coast, one company has asked for an oil concession of approximately 25 million acres. However, until the regulations for the disposal of mineral rights underlying the waters of Canada are promulgated, no permits can be issued.

And in Washington, scepticism greeted a report that undersecretary of state Douglas Dillon had found Canadian opposition to the proposed conference weakening during his visit to Ottawa early this month.

However, I believe my question would more properly have fitted in under the administration of the new Parole Act or the operation of it. I think probably what I did was to ask my question under the wrong vote.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Will my hon.
friend put his question on the next item, namely item 706?
Yes.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Shall item 705 carry?

No, Mr. Chairman. Item 705, which concerns departmental administration, gives me the opportunity to bring up for the consideration of the minister a matter on which he made a statement in the House of Commons on January 29, namely the possible effect of the operation of certain United States anti-trust legislation on legitimate Canadian business activities. I should like to take advantage of this opportunity to say a few words on this question which is of both legal and political importance. The minister himself in New York a few weeks ago made a strong statement with regard to United States policy and United States attitudes on this matter.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I rise on a point of order. I do not wish to minimize for a moment the importance of the topic the Leader of the Opposition wishes to discuss. However, I point out that the item relates to departmental administration; and if you will look at the details at page 6, you will see that it relates to the expenses of the correctional planning committee.

Supply-Justice
This is a supplementary estimate brought in for the specific purpose of enabling the department to meet the expenses of this committee which was appointed to advise as to the implementation of the Fauteux report in certain aspects. It is therefore, I submit, not a general item under departmental administration of such a nature as to make it possible for the general discussion of all matters coming within the administration of my department. The main estimates for the ensuing fiscal year will, of course, contain an administration item under which all aspects of my department can be debated, including the one which the Leader of the Opposition now wants to raise. However, on supplementary estimates, where items are brought forward for a specific purpose and not merely to expand the general vote under departmental administration, it has always been the practice of this house that the discussion of these items should relate to the specific purpose for which they are brought forward.

On the point of order, Mr. Chairman, may I say this. Surely it has been the practice of this house in discussions of the main estimates, the supplementary estimates and the final supplementary estimates, to permit on an item entitled "departmental administration", a wide-ranging discussion on the work of the department concerned.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Not on supplementary estimates.

That is a submission I am making to the chairman. This is a supplementary estimate but it is a supplementary estimate under the title "departmental administration". I would recall my statement in the house the other day when the minister made quite a long statement on the matter to which I referred. I said the other day that I would have an opportunity, I thought, to deal with this matter when the supplementary estimates were up for discussion. I would have thought, Mr. Chairman, that I was perfectly in order in dealing with this matter on an item under "departmental administration".

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
May I add a word on this subject, Mr. Chairman. The Leader of the Opposition has made the statement that it has been the practice of the house to have a wide-ranging discussion of departmental affairs on an item pertaining to any particular department both on the main estimates and on the supplementary estimates. May 1 say, Mr. Chairman, that has been the practice with regard to "departmental administration" only on the main estimates. But where supplementary estimates have been introduced late in the fiscal year, as is the present case, the practice of the house has

been-and it is completely in accord with the rule in this respect-that the discussion is confined to the item before the house. While the particular item comes under the heading of departmental administration, nevertheless this is an item for a particular purpose, and that particular purpose has been set out in the details on page 6. This relates to the correctional planning committee, which has nothing whatever to do with the matter that the Leader of the Opposition is proposing to discuss. The fact that the Leader of the Opposition mentioned several days ago that he intended to raise this matter on this item does not give it any validity; it does not make it in order. There was no undertaking given to him at that time by the house, or by anybody in it, that that privilege would be extended to him. It was not ruled to be a matter in order.
Mr. Chairman, I therefore ask, as we have been discussing the supplementary estimates a long time, and still have a number of them to deal with, that you rule that the only discussion admissible on this item is discussion pertaining to the expenses of the correctional planning committee, as indicated on page 6 of the details.

Mr. Chairman, if I may say a word, as a former member of the treasury board, about the point raised by the minister. The minister is, of course, aware that the treasury is not bound by the details. Once the money is voted for departmental administration it may be used for any aspect of departmental administration, notwithstanding the fact that it is the intention of the government at the time the estimates are submitted to use it-and I am not questioning the intention at the moment-for a particular purpose. I would admit at once that the Minister of Finance would be perfectly right in his contention if this were a specific item having to do only with correctional institutions. But this is an amount voted for the administration of the department, and it is within my recollection, and I am sure it must be within the recollection of the Minister of Finance also, that on many occasions on supplementary estimates, when the department has had to come back to ask for more money for departmental administration, some new question has arisen which did not exist at the time the main estimates were discussed. There has never been any objection taken in the house, in my experience, to a discussion of a matter of that kind, and therefore I submit that the Leader of the Opposition is in order.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
We are discussing the item of $15,200 which comes under the supplementary estimates. According to standing

order No. 59 (2) speeches in committee of the whole house must be strictly relevant to the item under consideration. This order will serve as the basis for what I shall now read, which appears in May's 16th edition at page 738 as follows:
On supplementary and excess grants.-Debate on supplementary and excess grants Is restricted to the particulars contained in the estimates on which those grants are sought, and to the application of the items which compose those grants; and the debate cannot touch the policy or the expenditure sanctioned, on other heads, by the estimate on which the original grant was obtained, except so far as such policy or expenditure is brought before the committee by the items contained in the supplementary or excess estimates.
Furthermore, I would like to read an observation made in 1954 by Mr. Abbott, as reported at page 3429 of Hansard for March 29:
I indicated that the main line of inquiry in the consideration of these estimates should be directed to why we require this extra money, because almost any major item involves the whole policy of that particular section, and perhaps we should have half a dozen debates on that during the year. I do not know. But it does not make for very orderly debate.
In conclusion, it is my impression that at the present time we must confine this debate to supplementary estimate No. 705 for a sum of $15,200 without entering into the general aspects of the Department of Justice. I therefore would like to ask hon. members to please confine the debate and their remarks to the assessment under discussion at this time.
Mr. Chairman, would you hear me on the point which you have so ably dealt with?

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Yes, indeed.

I have just been reading May which Your Honour has also quoted to the committee. Your Honour read the first paragraph which, on first reading, seemed to support the interpretation Your Honour has given to it. However, in small print it goes on to say:
This practice has been consistently upheld in committee of supply by the chairman, and in answer to a question put to him by the Chancellor of the Exchequer on 3 March 1893, the Speaker ruled as follows . . . Undoubtedly, of late years a certain limitation has been enforced upon the discussion of supplementary estimates. As a general rule, on the supplementary estimates it is in order to discuss only the particular items which constitute the supplementary estimates and the subheads of the original estimates can only be referred to so far as they are involved in the fair discussion of the points contained in the items asked for in the supplementary estimates.
Then it goes on:
Of course, it is quite obvious that it should be improper, as a general rule, to raise on a supplementary estimate the whole question of policy
Supply-Justice
involved in the original estimate; and, as I have stated, the discussion is properly confined to the items of the supplementary estimate. I think however, that I ought to state that items of supplementary estimates may raise in themselves questions of policy-
That is the very point that I think is before us now, because the policy of the department is determined by the administrative item. I am sure Your Honour, even in the short experience you have had in this house, has had an opportunity of seeing how the departmental estimates are devised. There is the administrative item and then the various subdivisions which relate to particular items. But the question of policy is one which is determined by the main item, the administrative item, which itself is not divisible, and it could not be argued that what I have read, and what Your Honour has read, except for the last matter, really touches the point at all. Otherwise we should be precluded from dealing with it. As it says here, "items of supplementary estimates may raise in themselves questions of policy." It goes on:
-but the interpretation whether they do raise questions of policy or not, must clearly be left to the chairman of committees.
We are on the only item that does involve a question of policy, and that is the administrative item itself. This $15,200 which is covered by this item need not be expended for this particular purpose. As the member for Bonavista-Twillingate said, it could be transferred at ministerial discretion for some other purpose under the administrative item. I do not think that by any stretch of the imagination could it be interpreted that our practice here at any time under supplementary or under main estimates has been that when we reach the administrative item any member is precluded from general discussion. What Your Honour has read does clearly apply to every other item of the further supplementary estimate sheet that is before us. There is no administrative item under agriculture or under the C.B.C. When we came to the C.B.C. item which was a grant toward the anticipated deficit of a particular service of the C.B.C. we permitted the widest discussion.
You were out of order.

Someone said we were out of order. Having taken that position on that item it would be very difficult for us I submit with great respect to deny an hon. member the opportunity of discussing under departmental administration policies that do come under what we mean by departmental administration in so far as it concerns the Department of Justice. The item for $15,200 is a variable item. It may be used for any particular purpose in the department

Supply-Justice
including, for instance, whatever expenses were involved in the necessary visit made by the Minister of Justice to Washington, although admittedly these expenses would not have been as high.
It would seem to me that the ruling Your Honour has given in this matter is understandable when one first looks at the language of May. The reason I asked Your Honour to allow me to look at the book which he so generously did was that I felt that it did refer not to departmental items so much as to specific items such as those which have been before us in these other items. For this reason I think Your Honour would want to give careful consideration to a ruling that would have such a restrictive effect.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
I have listened with great interest to the remarks made by the hon. member for Essex East and I should like to make a few comments in this regard. It is true that the quotation from May's 16th edition mentions that as a general rule the supplementary estimates do not permit a debate on a variety of subjects. Actually most of the rules of this house are based on precedents which do become more or less the laws which govern this chamber. In the case of supplementary estimates, although possibly it is not clearly defined that debate must be restricted only to the item under discussion and perhaps discussion may take place on a number of other matters relating to the supplementary estimates, hon. members must agree that it is preferable for orderly debate if the discussion be limited to the item under consideration.
For instance, the hon. member for Essex East referred to the wide discussion which took place on the item relating to the C.B.C. True enough, there was a wide debate on this matter which was in fact completely out of order. As everyone knows the debate became somewhat heated at one point and the Chair had to rule out of order all of the debate that was not relevant to the item under discussion. From now on it will be absolutely necessary to rule in the same fashion and that is to limit all debate to the relevancy of the subject.
In this case I have read in my ruling the statement that was made by the deputy chairman in 1954. I shall not read it again but I shall mention to the committee that there are other occasions when the chairman ruled in the same fashion. Hon. members may refer to page 2393 of Hansard for March 25, 1955, to pages 2467 and 2503 of Hansard for March 21 and 22, 1956, and also to page 2432 of Hansard for March 18, 1957. For all these reasons I must adhere to my

original ruling that the debate be entirely relevant to the item under discussion.
However, if the Minister of Justice is agreeable to answering some of the questions of the Leader of the Opposition and if it is the pleasure of the committee to permit him to do so, I am quite agreeable to letting the hon. member ask these questions. I must, however, inform hon. gentlemen that if the debate gets out of hand, hon. members will be called back to order.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, I think you have pretty well put the Minister of Justice on the spot and the only answer I may make, if I may put it that way, to your suggestion is that as Minister of Justice I should be the last person to suggest a breach of the rules of this committee. I must say that to try to have a debate now on a matter such as that which the Leader of the Opposition seeks to raise on an item of $15,200 relating to the correctional planning committee is in my view, and in accordance with your ruling, so far out of order that I would not take it on myself to ask the other hon. members of the committee to countenance such a wide and sweeping breach of the rules.

Mr. Chairman, of course we accept without reservation your ruling in this matter. Perhaps I go a little too far when I say without reservation, but we do accept it. I know you were inspired by fairness in making it. I could not, however, accept the suggestion which you made in good faith to restrict myself to a few questions directed to the minister because the matter is of such importance that I think it requires more than a few questions. I can only say that I regret I will not have an opportunity at this time to deal to the best of my ability with the long statement the minister made on this important matter the other day in the house under motions which did not provide an opportunity for reply and which contained what I thought were some remarks which should be answered at the earliest possible opportunity.

Mr. Chairman, I find myself in the same position as the Leader of the Opposition. I have to forgo certain remarks I was going to make on this subject, too. However, dealing specifically with this item, I shall be absolutely in order, as I always am, in asking the Minister of Justice to give us some information on the operations of the correctional planning committee and the reason for the requirement of additional funds.
I take it that this is the committee which is to function in implementing and studying

the recommendations of various royal commission reports that have had to do with institutions of correction and probation and as to the division of jurisdiction in care as between the provincial and federal governments. I know that for a long time a great many hon. members and many individuals and organizations outside of this chamber have been anxiously awaiting the time when they could learn what action is to be taken on the recommendations made by various commissions or whether the reports of those bodies were just going to gather dust on the bookshelf.
In view of the fact that this committee has been appointed we will all be most anxious to learn just how far the negotiations have gone with the provinces with respect to agreement concerning the bringing in of necessary legislation at the provincial and federal level required for the implementation of these recommendations. We would also be interested in knowing the opinion of the Minister of Justice as to how long it will require before decisions can be reached concerning changes in legislation and the planning of new institutions or the remodelling of existing institutions in order to take care of the overcrowded situation that obtains all across Canada at the present time.
In the same connection, I know that we from British Columbia would appreciate hearing from the minister as to whether this planning committee had anything to do, or has anything to do now with the opening of the new institution, if I can put it in these terms, on Vancouver island where we have what I think is an endeavour to establish something new in this country in the way of an open institution,-I believe that is the proper word-as compared with a completely walled-in and large institution. I should also like to know whether or not consideration is being given by the correctional committee, not to the temporary use of that location on Vancouver island, which has been unused although in federal hands for many years, but to carry on on an extended basis and in line with modern penology throughout the world.
In asking for this $15,200 for departmental administration, and for this purpose I think the minister has opened up a most interesting and informative field, and one which until now both the house and the country has been kept a great deal in the dark about. In asking for this supplementary vote the minister has opened up the opportunity to give us the fullest possible information as to what has been going on and what is going on at the present time in planning for the future.
Supply-Justice
I think the minister could give us a statement now about what this particular vote is for so that we can determine whether or not he is any more in order than was the Leader of the Opposition.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I appreciate always the interest taken by all hon. members in this house in the matter of correctional planning, as it has come to be called. This arises largely out of the report of the Fauteux commission and the plans that have to be made and are being made to implement certain of those recommendations. We have had expressions of interest and concern and, indeed, very constructive suggestions in this field, from a large number of members of the house in all parties.
I regret that the hon. member for Vancouver East has said that the house is being kept in the dark. Certainly, as far as I am concerned, I have never failed to answer any questions to the best of my ability. It is true that I did have to say for some months that our plans were entirely in the formative stage and therefore I could not give very many concrete answers. Now, however, the time has arrived when for the first time our plans have advanced to the point where we have this correctional planning committee appointed hard at work and I am able to give the committee a progress report on the work that has been done to get things ready to carry into effect some of the very important recommendations made by the Fauteux commission.
I should say also that at every stage when any step was taken when the house was not in session, that was felt by myself and my colleagues to be important enough to warrant a special statement, we released statements to the press so that as far as possible the country was kept fully informed as to what was being done.
I shall now try as briefly as possible to summarize the present position. The committee will recall that the recommendations of the Fauteux commission in their entirety involved a large measure of agreement between the dominion and the provinces because in order to implement them in so far as they related to matters which were in the provincial field we can only, of course, proceed if we do have the agreement of the provinces.
I found in June, 1957, that no steps had been taken to convene a meeting with provincial authorities to discuss all the ramifications of the implementation of the Fauteux recommendations. We had ourselves as a new government to assess the situation with which we were confronted. We found that

Supply-Justice
not only were we confronted with the problems arising out of those very important recommendations, with respect to which no consultations had been initiated with the provinces, but we were also confronted with the problems arising from the fact that in the field for which the dominion government is already responsible, let alone any enlarged field for which it might assume responsibility, things had reached almost emergency proportions.
The hon. gentleman who last spoke referred to the fact that we have a situation of overcrowding in our federal penal institutions. That is correct. The situation has reached almost emergency proportions. We were able-and this was an incidental fact-to take care of the overcrowding situation initially by the fact that at about the time we took office, or shortly thereafter, it was arranged that Her Majesty the Queen would visit Canada and the government decided at that time to give an amnesty-
Is that why she is coming back?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
-to prisoners in penitentiary. These are interesting sidelights that flow from some of these other activities. That relieved the overcrowding situation. That, of course, was not the reason why the amnesty was given but it was one indirect result. But ever since October of 1957, we have been faced with a continuation of the problem in respect of the overcrowding of the penal institutions under the jurisdiction of the federal government, until now it has reached proportions where we have had to take emergency action with respect to the situation in St. Vincent de Paul in Montreal and the British Columbia penitentiary. In both those institutions the overcrowding had reached the point where considerations of prudent administration from the point of view of preserving order in the institutions themselves, as well as regard for the proper conditions under which inmates should be housed, would not permit any longer the deferment of measures to deal with the situation. Perhaps I should not go into any further details here because this is covered under two items of the penitentiary supplementary estimates which will come up later. But for St. Vincent de Paul and British Columbia we have set up temporary institutions to relieve the overcrowding.
Now I mention that subject only to bring the committee into the picture of the extent of the problem with which we were confronted. Not only, did we have this problem of what to do with regard to the increased jurisdiction that the Fauteux commission recommended we should assume, and all the problems of agreement with the provinces

on that, and the new institutions that would have to be constructed or taken over if we did agree with the provinces and assumed this responsibility, but in addition we had the current and increasing problem of the tremendous growth in penitentiary population within the categories-that is, those serving sentences of two years and over-for which in any event we have responsibility.
I think we have moved as rapidly as could be expected to deal with both of these problems. Penal institutions are enormously expensive to construct. I feel that the time has arrived in Canada when we should examine seriously the design of the institutions we are building, although here again perhaps I shold defer the detailed discussion until we reach the penitentiary item. But this is only one of the aspects of the problems that we have had. We have had to take a completely new look at the type of institutions we are providing for those now under federal authority.
In addition, we have had to look at the types of reform programs that we should institute in connection with the added number of inmates for whom we would be assuming responsibility if the Fauteux recommendations are to be implemented, and all the related problems of parole services, integration of the parole service with the probation services of the provinces and co-ordination of our efforts in parole with the efforts of the voluntary after-care agencies, bearing in mind that the work both of the parole service and of the voluntary agencies will be greatly increased when in fact we take over the additional number of prisoners which will be the result of adopting the recommendations of the Fauteux committee.
The first thing we had to do was to arrive at a decision in principle on the part of the dominion government. Would we accept the recommendations of the Fauteux committee? If we accepted them, what would that involve in the way of financial expenditure on new institutions? What would it involve in the way of expenditure in connection with the new staff that we would have to recruit? What would it involve in the way of the training of the new staff that we would have to recruit in order to administer the physical problem presented by the number of inmates and the reform problem presented by the new program that we wanted to institute?
It would have been completely foolish, I think, for us to have rushed ahead and entered into discussions with the provinces on the Fauteux report before we had assessed for ourselves those steps which we would have to take in order to implement that report if agreement should be arrived at. We had to make that assessment first of all. Some

time ago my colleagues arrived at agreement and authorized me to communicate with the provinces to the effect that the government was prepared to accept in principle the recommendations of the Fauteux committee. We had made a preliminary study of what was involved physically and financially and had decided that we would accept it, that it was in the interests of the country to do so and in the interests of modern penal reform and modern penal methods.
So an invitation was extended to the attorneys general of all the provinces and other provincial ministers interested in or responsible for prison matters, and a conference was held in Ottawa in October of last year. A full statement was issued at the conclusion of the conference so I will not go into too great detail here beyond reminding the committee that I am extremely happy to be able to report that unanimous agreement was arrived at in that conference on the general principle of the implementation of the Fauteux committee recommendations in so far as those proposals related to the assumption by the dominion government of responsibility for persons sentenced to terms of over six months. There were some details in that connection which can be found if hon. members care to consult the communique issued at the close of the conference.
Has my hon. friend given the names of the members of the committee?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
Not yet. The conference I am discussing at the moment is the conference between myself and my officials on the one hand and the provincial attorneys general and other provincial ministers on the other hand.
It is true that some reservations were expressed by some of the provinces, notably my own province of British Columbia, but in general it is correct to say that there was unanimous agreement within the areas I have described. Having obtained the approval of the provinces, it was necessary immediately after that to set up a planning group within our own staff to work out the details of the arrangements that will have to be carried out in order to make this agreement in principle a reality in fact. As I announced through the medium of a press release some time ago a correctional planning committee was appointed consisting of Mr. A. J. MacLeod, Q.C., director of the criminal law section of the Department of Justice and previously director of the remission service in my department; Colonel J. R. Stone, ex-provost marshal of the Canadian army; and Mr. J. A. McLaughlin, assistant commissioner of penitentiaries.
Supply-Justice
That committee has been instructed to carry out its planning in accordance with fairly lengthy and full terms of reference. I have the terms of reference before me. If they are of interest to the committee I could read them but it is a fairly lengthy document and if the committee wishes I can table it so that the terms of reference can be studied at leisure.
Paraphrase it.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
In general the instructions to the committee are divided into a number of sections: institutional, narcotic drugs, correctional workers, after-care of inmates, research and public education. In connection with the institutional aspect of planning the committee is instructed to plan a program for the custody, treatment and training of adult offenders with the object of achieving the reform and ultimate rehabilitation of as large a number of inmates as possible on the basis that the dominion will assume responsibility for persons sentenced under federal laws to terms of one year or more and that sentences under federal laws of more than six months but less than one year will be eliminated.
Second, the committee is instructed to plan a system of diversified institutions by means of which, in accordance with generally accepted modern correctional principles the program can be carried out effectively and efficiently, including recommendations for the design and location of such new institutions as may be necessary and the phasing of a building program.
Third, the committee is to formulate suitable proposals whereby effect may be given to the agreement reached at the dominion-provincial conference of October 13 and 14, 1958, relating to the custody of convicted persons who are mentally ill, the custody of convicted persons who are under the age of: 16 years and the custody of female prisoners.. Perhaps I should pause there to say that it. was agreed in principle at the dominion-provincial conference that new arrangements should be made for the custody of the three categories of persons whom I have mentioned.
Next-this is still under "institutional"- commencing immediately and in consultation with the commissioner of penitentiaries the committee is to make recommendations concerning the location, design and function of any new or enlarged institutions or projects that are necessary or desirable to relieve existing overcrowded conditions in Canadian penitentiaries, bearing in mind the necessity of integrating any new or expanded institutions into the over-all program and building plans envisaged in the earlier parts of their instruction.

Supply-Justice
The question of narcotic drugs is perhaps not immediately relevant to the discussion so I will skip that part. Perhaps the committee may agree to my tabling these terms of reference later because, although I think I could say that this is technically an interdepartmental document which would normally be privileged, in view of the interest that there is in this program I would be quite prepared to table the instructions in full if hon. members so desire.
Under the heading of "correctional workers" the committee is instructed to survey the present and future needs for trained correctional workers in the federal correctional field and to compile information received from the provincial governments concerning their needs for correctional workers and the available resources for their training. The committee is also to plan a co-operative program with the provincial governments and, where appropriate, with the voluntary after-care agencies under which we may provide facilities for advanced training in correctional work. Also, in consultation with the commissioner of penitentiaries the committee is to plan an improved program of in-service training for custodial officers employed in the penitentiary service.
Under the heading of "after-care of inmates" the committee is instructed to survey -the work done in this field by the after-care agencies, to consult with the new national parole board and with all others concerned and to make recommendations for expanding the work in that field. They are instructed also to make recommendations whereby the operations of the federal parole service and provincial probation service may be better co-ordinated to promote efficiency and economy in the after care of released inmates.
Then, there are instructions with regard to research, and with regard to public education or information concerning the program we (have under way. The committee has further been instructed, in the course of its planning, fo visit each of the provinces of Canada to determine the nature of the existing operations of our own penitentiaries branch there, and the views of the local penitentiary officials *concerning possible future operations and locations for those operations. They have been instructed also to discuss the type of institutional program now being carried on by the provinces and the location and possible suitability for federal purposes of existing provincial institutions because we may well have -to take over, if the provinces agree, some of their existing institutions, as and when we assume responsibility for some of the inmates *who are under provincial responsibility.

The committee has been instructed also to ascertain the views of local authorities concerning future programs and types, location and suitability of future institutions. They have been instructed to make certain travels abroad, particularly in the United States and in the United Kingdom to examine the nature of the penal institutions in those countries and the principles upon which those institutions are administered, having in mind of course the emphasis in the United Kingdom is on probation, the Borstal system and so on.
I recognize that this is a lengthy summary, and I am sorry. However, this is a huge field. It is lengthy, and yet it is still only a summary of the instructions we have given to the committee. Finally, the committee has been instructed that, if it is at all possible, that they must complete their program of travel and investigation by June 30 of this year, and that they will be expected to submit their report and recommendations, if possible by December 30 of this year.
Is the travelling all in Canada?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
No, as I explained just a moment ago, most of their travelling will be within Canada, but they are instructed to go particularly to the United States and the United Kingdom as well.
This then, Mr. Chairman, is a summary of the scope of the work of the correctional planning committee. I have been asked also whether the committee is to give any consideration to the problem which we now face with respect to the overcrowding in our present institutions. Yes, they are. In the course of their travels they will be expected to visit Canadian penitentiaries in order to assess the situation there. We did refer to them, as a special matter, the situation in British Columbia and at St. Vincent de Paul where, as I have said, the greatest degree of overcrowding exists. It is due to the committee, in large part, that the suggestion for the use of William Head was put forward.

That is the old
immigration building?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
The William Head institution is the old immigration and health centre, and it was under the jurisdiction of my colleague the Minister of National Health and Welfare. In connection with St. Vincent de Paul, we have arranged with the Department of National Defence to take over temporarily the army camp at Valleyfield. I can give more details on both William Head and Valleyfield under the supplementary item of penitentiaries which will be reached in a few moments.

The final question is whether or not it is intended to carry on the use of the William Head type of institution which is now being established there. I should say in answer to that question, that it is essential to make clear that in so far as William Head and Valley field are concerned, those are only temporary measures to relieve overcrowding. They are not to be regarded in any sense as the beginning of the new institutions. It may be that we will find, when the committee completes its study, that William Head or Valleyfield may fit into the over-all plans that they then recommend. However, I have made clear to all those with whom I have corresponded, and it is certainly clear in the minds of the departmental officials, that William Head and Valleyfield are not the commencement of any new plan. They are temporary measures to relieve emergency overcrowding which we had inherited. I would not want at this stage, before the committee has had time to make a sensible over-all plan, to commit ourselves to William Head or Valleyfield, and perhaps later on find that they did not fit in with the over-all plan and yet, by reason of committing ourselves, we had perhaps distorted the program we would eventually like to carry out. These two moves, then, are entirely of a temporary and emergency nature. Of course, we hope to get a good deal of benefit from the experience of the decentralized operation of two of the main penitentiaries in Canada.
I believe I have answered the questions so far. I think the committee will agree with me when I say there was throughout the country a great deal of approbation of the appointments made to the correctional planning committee, and the country expects a great deal from the work of this committee. From my knowledge of the gentlemen concerned and of the way in which they are going about their planning work, the vigour and enthusiasm with which they are approaching their task, I think I can safely say the government and the country will not be disappointed by the results that the committee produces.

The minister
