speaks of the overcrowding of these institutions as one of the considerations before the planning committee. I presume that the committee will have in mind finding some place, not merely to house the bodies of prisoners who are of a certain age, but the provision of additional facilities which will take into account the segregation of certain classes of prisoners, particularly young people, many of whom find themselves lodged in penitentiaries. The minister did not make
Supply-J ustice
clear in the statement I heard whether or not that is an objective which the committee will bear in mind.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
I think I did make it clear,
but I think the hon. gentleman was called out of the house for a few minutes. I pointed out that it was one of the instructions of the committee to formulate in the planning suitable proposals whereby effect may be given to the agreement reached at the dominion-provincial conference of October 13 and 14, 1958, relating to the custody of convicted persons who are mentally ill, the custody of convicted persons who are under 16 years of age and the custody of female prisoners.

I should like to ask the
Minister of Justice a few questions with reference to his remarks, particularly since I am interested in and have worked with young people in the provinces of Alberta and Saskatchewan who have from time to time broken the rules of society and become incarcerated in our institutions. If I understood the minister correctly, his department is now endeavouring to work out arrangements with the provinces to assume responsibility for those prisoners who have been given sentences greater than six months. I take it that the federal government would then become financially responsible for those institutions in which a person was incarcerated for a length of time greater than six months?

That is correct, Mr. Chairman. Of course, the details and the terms under which we will assume that responsibility is amongst those matters which have been referred to the correctional planning committee. They will be entering into negotiations with the provinces as to the basis upon which we will assume this responsibility.
Perhaps I should say it is our plan, when this over-all program goes into effect, that sentences under federal statutes for terms of less than 12 months will be eliminated because it is our feeling that inasmuch as federal institutions will become in large part, not exclusively but in large part, reform institutions, sentences of less than 12 months would not warrant committal to a federal reform institution.

There is another question I should like to ask. The minister mentioned overcrowded conditions at Montreal and Winnipeg. I wonder whether he could give us some information as to the conditions at the penitentiary at Prince Albert in Saskatchewan. Conditions in the penitentiary in Alberta are not overcrowded because we have not a penitentiary. About 65 per cent of the inmates in Saskatchewan come from

Supply-Justice
the province of Alberta. I wonder whether the minister would be prepared to tell us today what the situation is in the Prince Albert penitentiary.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: May I suggest to the hon. gentleman that he might defer detailed questions until we get to items 707 and 708 under the heading "Penitentiaries". In general, however, in response to his question, I can say that all our federal penitentiaries are overcrowded and the matter is one of real concern. The two worst were at Montreal and British Columbia. Speaking from recollection I would say that Dorchester and Prince Albert are about next in order. As I recall it, the situation in Manitoba is about the best. There is overcrowding at Kingston, but that overcrowding will be relieved shortly by the coming into operation of the new institution at Joyceville, 11 miles from Kingston, which institution will be completed and will come into full operation during the current year.

I thank the minister. I have one other question I should like to ask. This matter is often raised and we are asked about it by our constituents and sometimes in our practice of law. Under the new system that is being implemented under the committee just how long would a person be obliged to serve in a penitentiary a sentence he has been given before he can make application for parole? This matter may come under the next item, but while I was on my feet, as the minister covered part of that field, I felt that I might ask it here.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: At the present time there is a rule of thumb that an inmate must have served half his sentence before his file is closely examined for parole. I have discussed this matter with Mr. Streets, the chairman of the new parole board, and have asked him to take a look at this rule of thumb and to keep it in mind. I am not satisfied that a rule of thumb is the kind of rule you want when you are dealing with human factors. I have asked him to keep that in mind and I find that, in general terms, he agrees with my approach and will bear it in mind when he is drafting the new regulations under which the national parole board will operate.

In reference to that matter, Mr. Chairman, may I say this. I do not know how exact these figures would be but in discussing this problem with the John Howard Society in Calgary I found they went so far as to say that we are facing a situation of parole where 80 per cent of those who have been given an opportunity of parole do not return to the penitentiary whereas it is in

reverse when they have not had the opportunity of parole. That is why I was interested as to when they could make application for parole.

There is one small matter I think we might deal with under this item. It was occasioned by the comment the minister made when he was informing us of the provisions with reference to this committee. It has reference to drug addiction and drug addicts and the large field covered. I wonder whether the minister under this item would be in a position to relate what additional steps have been taken since the last time this matter was discussed toward the idea of setting up a hospital or clinic or separate institution in which to deal with or to house drug addicts and to assist them in becoming non-addicts upon their release?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I answered a somewhat similar question dealing with this subject asked by the hon. member for Vancouver East on the orders of the day and I am not able to add much to what I said then. The subject is being studied now and when I say "studied" I do not mean I am putting it off. I mean it is being studied by the officials of my department and those of the Department of National Health and Welfare; and with the knowledge and consent of the Minister of National Health and Welfare it has also been referred as a specific item to the correctional planning committee for study and report. As I said this morning, it is a field in which it is important that we make progress, and yet a field in which it is difficult to obtain agreement as to the direction in which that progress should be made, because there are wide and strongly held differences of opinion in this field.

Item agreed to.
706. Remission service-further amount required for Parole Act administration and to authorize the expenditure, for the purposes of the said act, of moneys provided for the remission service by the Appropriation Act No. 5, 1958, $28,000.

Under this item I should like to raise questions with regard to the practice of commuting death sentences to life imprisonment, one which has grown up in recent years. The committee will recall that the other day, in answer to a question asked by the hon. member for Hochelaga-and I am quoting from page 852 of Hansard-the minister gave the answer that 21 capital sentences were considered by the governor in council since June, 1957, and that 17 of those 21 were commuted to life imprisonment. I believe that only in the case of four of these 21 sentences was a recommendation for mercy received by the cabinet. Mr. Chairman, the question is not one of whether or not to

-abolish the death penalty. The question is whether, if action is to be taken in that direction, it should be taken by means of executive action.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I am sorry to interrupt; that is why I have allowed this much of the speech to go by. I hesitated to rise on a point of order again but the Leader of the Opposition is now discussing the question of commutation of death sentences. That is something which is done in cabinet and not by the remission service. And especially if, as I now sense, the direction of the hon. gentleman's question is going to lead us into a discussion of the principle on which the death sentence should be confirmed or commuted or anything related to capital punishment, I reluctantly draw your attention, Mr. Chairman, to the fact that such discussion would be out of order under the present item.

The reason I raise this matter under this item is a clear and indeed an obvious one. We are dealing with the remission service. It is the function of the remission service to consider applications for remission of sentences. If death sentences are going to be commuted to life imprisonment, as has been done recently, this action will undoubtedly add to the work of the remission service for which an appropriation is being requested under this vote. Under the Parole Act, as the minister, of course, knows-I refer to section 7 (a) of the Parole Act- there are periodic reviews of sentences.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: On the point of order may I say this. There are not periodic views of death sentences. Death sentences automatically come before council or the cabinet and the decision whether to confirm or to commute is made there. That decision is not made by the remission service.

Of course that statement is correct, Mr. Chairman. But a sentence which is commuted to life imprisonment brings the prisoner within the ambit of the action of the remission service. Surely that fact permits us to talk about the commutation of death sentences which adds, in this case, 17 prisoners who will, in due course-perhaps after 15 years-be eligible for parole and whose sentences will at that time be reviewed by those who are administering this particular act.
All I want to say, and it will only take me a minute to say it, is that if this additional work is to be given to the remission service by the commutation of sentences, then that step should be taken by parliamentary discussion and decision and the necessary amendment of our present legislation, and not by
Supply-Justice
executive action of the government. That is the point I want to make.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I do not know whether what the hon. gentleman suggests is that we should not commute sentences because it might cost the country something. I hope that is not the suggestion.
No, it is not.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: If the suggestion is not as I have suggested, then it must be that the matter should be dealt with by way of statute, which amounts also to a suggestion that the governor in council should not continue to exercise the prerogative of mercy. The hon. gentleman and the committee will realize, this being a prerogative, that each individual case is dealt with on its merits, as I have had occasion to say recently when questioned on a television broadcast.

Mr. Chairman, under this particular item I would like to make a suggestion, and I hope I shall receive an answer of some sort from the minister, although he may not be in a position to be definite about it. The old act, as I recall, allows for a maximum membership on the parole board of five.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Yes, a membership of five; that is correct.

It allows for a maximum membership of five on the board and there are presently four members. In view of the comments which were made earlier under the preceding item that the department or the federal government will be extending its jurisdiction over sentences to a point where they will be reduced from the present two years to one year, and so on, it would bring far more women prisoners under the jurisdiction of the commissioners and the department than there are at the present time. I believe at the moment there are some 98 or 100 women in the women's penitentiary at Kingston. Now what an addition of one year would mean I do not know, but I am sure that it will mean that there will be far more women considered by the parole board for parole. In view of that, I wonder whether the minister will reserve, if he has not already done so, that additional space on the parole board for a woman? Would he consider the appointment of a woman to fill that position so that the woman's point of view may be present on the parole board?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
I appreciate the remarks that the hon. gentleman has made, and I share with him the feeling that this is a place where the point of view of women should be increasingly recognized, and through the parole board it should be given effect. I

Supply-J ustice
cannot, as I stand here today, give a firm commitment that if and when an appointment is made to the fifth vacancy it will be a woman, but I can tell the hon. gentleman that I have received many representations to the effect that the vacancy should be filled by a woman, and those representations will be borne in mind if and when the appointment comes to be made.
One further point. Could the minister indicate whether it will not be a man?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: It will be a Canadian.

Mr. Chairman, without having been sentenced I make periodic visits to the penitentiary, and I am one of the fortunate ones who can get in and out. As a matter of fact only three days before I left British Columbia for the opening of this House of Commons I visited the penitentiary of British Columbia, and there I met one of the old friends of the Minister of Justice. I do not mean a personal friend, but a friend who has very often come to his notice, especially in the last session.
Liberal?

I did not ask him how he voted. At the present moment he has not a vote. My point has to do with the question of parole and revocation. In other words, I am referring to the Minister of Justice's old friend, Mr. Munavish, who had his ticket of leave cancelled last year. I promised that I would draw to the minister's attention at the earliest opportunity the fact that this man still maintains that he was wrongfully picked up and was not guilty of the breaking of his ticket parole as charged. He maintains that he has never had a proper opportunity of giving an explanation, shall I say, or answer the accusation made against him, and therefore that he was unjustly recommitted to an indefinite term to the penitentiary. As I think the hon. minister knows, I have quite a few remission cases, and when I meet these prisoners in the penitentiary, or communicate with them in correspondence, I am pretty blunt with them. If I think they are trying to lead me astray I let them know point blank where they get off. I can assure the minister that I did the same thing when I met Mr. Munavish, and the warder who was present with me can confirm what I say. At that time I was not satisfied with the answers I got.
Since arriving back here in Ottawa I have heard from Mr. Munavish, who admitted that perhaps he was wrong in trying to evade the questions I asked. If the answers he now gives and which I did not receive when I

first saw him are correct, then I think it might be in the interests of justice to give that man once again an opportunity of answering the questions which were put to him. In view of the very kind offer made by the minister last year, would he send in an official to personally interview this man? I would like to ask whether consideration could be given to that matter. In addition, can the minister state with regard to this new consideration of parole, of remission or ticket of leave, that there is going to be very considerable thought given as to the basis on which prisoners can have their ticket of leave completely cancelled without there being a sense that full justice has not been done, or that injustice has been done.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, as to the specific case the hon. gentleman refers to, I will be glad to refer it, in my turn, to the chairman of the parole board. The board is now set up and will commence to function under the new act which comes into force on the 15th of this month. I will ask the chairman of the parole board to look at the remarks of the hon. gentleman, look at the past record, and in the light of what has been said to have another look at the Munavish case.
With respect to the general problem of the recommittal of parolees, this is an area where it is difficult always to expect complete agreement. The general principle is that a person out on parole is not a free person who is deprived of a right when he is recommitted. The fact is that he is a man still under sentence, who has been given a licence to spend the rest of his sentence at liberty so long as he complies with certain conditions which may be laid down, and so long as the parole authorities are satisfied that there is no danger to society in his continuing to be at large. It is on that basis that I think it would be impossible to say that a parolee who is ordered for recommittal is entitled, as it were, to a full trial in the full implication of those words, because he is not charged with anything. He is not charged with a new offence.
It is a matter of judgment.
The parole authorities may come to the conclusion that-perhaps because he may have taken up again with his former associates with whom he fell into a life of crime originally, or because of other indications- that if they leave him at large any longer he will in fact commit another crime, that in his best interests and those of society the wisest thing that could be done is to put him back into prison for the time being. These are matters of judgment, as I say, and I do not think we will always get agreement. Here again, I do not like the

idea of committing or recommitting a man without giving him the fullest possible information as to the basis on which he is committed or recommitted. I have asked the chairman of the parole board to look at the problem also and when he comes to draft his regulations to see what can be done and what latitude can be allowed with respect to the circumstances under which, and the information which will be made available to a prisoner or a parolee who is ordered to be recommitted.

Mr. Chairman, the Minister of Justice has mentioned the chairman of the parole board and I would be very remiss if I did not say a word of congratulation to the minister on the appointment of Magistrate George Streets of Welland as chairman of that board. Coming from Welland county I have known this gentleman for many years. Although we differed politically we were always the best of friends and I wish to tell the minister that he has made a splendid choice in this appointment. Magistrate Streets was always held in high respect in Welland county and did a fine job as a young magistrate. I know he will win commendation as chairman of the board and fill that office not only with honour and respect to himself but to the minister and the government as well.

Item agreed to.
B-Penitentiaries
707. Operation and maintenance of penitentiaries -further amount required, $151,394.

Mr. Chairman, we have just passed an item in relation to the parole legislation recently approved by the house. I think it is fair to say that item 707 and the previous items are inter-related in a very real way. I think it is also fair to say, as the minister said a few moments ago, that all the items under the supplementary estimates of the Department of Justice are inter-related. As recommendations with respect to parole legislation are implemented we hope to see the prison population falling within federal competence diminish and yet as the federal authorities take over a field previously held by provincial authorities this population might possibly increase.
I do not intend to open up a full discussion on modern penology or criminology methods under this item but I do feel a few brief remarks are definitely in order. The Minister of Justice has already stated that when he assumed his portfolio he found an unbelievable state of overcrowdedness in federal penitentiaries. I hope I am not introducing a partisan note when I voice a certain
Supply-Justice
degree of surprise that the past administration should have let the building aspect of Canadian penitentiaries deteriorate to such a great extent. No apparent attempt was made to keep up with modern methods of criminology in terms of the physical buildings. I am thinking particularly of the penitentiary at St. Vincent de Paul which I have personally visited. The conditions I found there not very long ago smacked of a bygone age.
I should like to introduce this general note into the discussion at this time. There are many important fields of governmental activity requiring public co-operation and understanding and this is also very true with respect to this aspect of the work of the Department of Justice. What we have to convey to the public is knowledge of the fact that any improvement in penology does not-

Order. I would ask hon. members to please follow the items as numbered in the supplementary estimates. We are presently discussing item No. 707 respecting the operation and maintenance of penitentiaries.

Mr. Chairman, I was just going to stress the fact that any improvement in the operation of the physical plant of our penitentiaries is most certainly related to modern methods of criminology. Many private organizations have approached me personally, as I know they have approached other hon. gentlemen, commending the present Minister of Justice for the new look that is obviously in vogue in his department.
Now you definitely are out of order.

I may be out of order but I would like to say this. When I saw the state of affairs existing with respect to Canadian penitentiaries at the end of the Liberal regime I could not help but think that the famous 19th century Liberals would have been rather surprised at the so-called party of reform in the mid-twentieth century. I cannot understand why the previous Liberal administration did not implement more of the recommendations contained in the Ar-chambault and Fauteux reports. I can say that the present administration intends to carry out the main recommendations of the Fauteux report and one can already see this in the supplementary estimates before us today. Expenditures are being made along these lines and this should win the wholehearted approval of this committee and the people of Canada.

Mr. Chairman, if I were a Liberal-heaven forbid-I might have some

Supply-Justice
cause to make a few comments concerning what the speaker who preceded me had to say. I wonder if we would be stretching a point in asking permission to consider the provisions of items Nos. 707 and 708 together because they are related. Item No. 707 refers to the operation and maintenance of penitentiaries and item No. 708 refers to construction, improvements and equipment. I imagine item 708 is the reason for the additional amount required in 707. If it could be viewed in that light we might discuss it more intelligently.

Hon.
members of the committee have heard the suggestion of the hon. member for Skeena. Is the committee agreeable to discussing the two items together?
Agreed.

Thank you very much, Mr. Chairman, and members of the committee. There are just one or two matters that require clarification. The minister was kind enough to make a brief reference to the additional expenditures required. In examining the details listed on page 7 I observe that they refer to St. Vincent de Paul and British Columbia. Doubtless these institutions were more over-crowded than others. I take it from the minister's remarks that the additional buildings that were constructed were of a temporary nature and were not necessarily to be the pattern for any future operation of penitentiaries or any security program. Can the minister tell us what type of accommodation has been provided at these two institutions as a result of this vote?
The next item listed refers to the construction of additional buildings at penitentiaries. Can the minister say if this refers to the New Westminster penitentiary or simply the one at William Head to which he referred?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, dealing with the last part of the question first, so far as the item referring to British Columbia is concerned it is exclusively restricted to British Columbia. We may not find it possible to spend any more money on old buildings because you can only renovate, rehabilitate and modernize old buildings up to a certain point and after that you do not get a return for what you are spending. We do not want to spend money on old buildings because we know we are going to have to build a number of new institutions.
With regard to the type of building required at William Head and Valleyfield, at William Head we have taken over a portion of the quarantine station operated by the Department of National Health and Welfare

which is estimated to be able to accommodate up to 100 prisoners. The buildings themselves are not being extensively altered. We were fortunate in finding something that, for the type of inmate which will be sent there, is almost immediately suitable and, as the hon. member for Vancouver East pointed out, it forms what you might call an open type of institution. Those who will be sent there to relieve the overcrowding are those who are nearing the end of their sentences or, alternatively, those on short sentences and who do not require any great security measures to be taken with respect to them. We have not had to make too many alterations at William Head. We have had to do some cleaning up, modernizing and minor adjustments.
I would also like to make clear again that we are not committing ourselves here to William Head but because of the type of institution that we happen to be running there, because of the type of inmate we will be sending there, we expect to get a very great deal of benefit from that experience in moving toward a more open type of institution.

On this most interesting point that has been raised by the Minister of Justice, may we ask him to rise and expatiate a little bit more. According to the information given to us a few minutes ago, he does not expect any reports until at least September of this year on the type of construction, place of construction and so forth. After that is received the government will have to give consideration to it. After that is done there will be the drafting of plans and after that there will be construction. I am afraid it is going to be quite a long time, even with the minister hurrying up as much as he possibly can, before very much can be done in the way of alleviating the new scale of overcrowding of the penitentiaries.
As I mentioned a few moments ago, I was in a British Columbia penitentiary a few days before coming down to Ottawa. Not only have they had to open up new dormitories, or expand new dormitories, but they have actually had to place the beds in the corridors in front of the cells. I can assure you, Mr. Chairman, that that does not make for a happy situation and if eastern Canada continues to send their criminals to British Columbia, where we have to sentence them to our penitentiaries, we are going to need more accommodation. There is no question about that, and we are going to need it in the near future.
Therefore, I would like to suggest-I hope it is in the minister's mind-that if anything additional at all is to be done in the existing

penitentiaries, as far as British Columbia is concerned,-I think it applies everywhere else-they try to do it on a dormitory basis, not only because it is cheaper but also because they only put in there those who have a good record and the aid to morale is terrific. The difference between those in the dormitories under very close supervision, of course,-and there are from 24 to 30 in the dormitories in the evening-and those who are locked up so many hours by themselves in a cell is startling.
In addition to this there is one other little point that I should like to mention. I will not take more than a couple of minutes to do it. I find I can only do it in one way and that is by making reference to the detail having to do with remuneration paid to inmates. I see that the vote amounts to $1,100. I want to use it as the basis for what I wish to say. Can consideration be given to perhaps making a policy change in the basis of paying remuneration to inmates? I should like to suggest that a change be made and I hope that my suggestions will be taken very seriously. I mentioned it once before. I should like the payment of remuneration to inmates to include as an entitlement a holdback, and the holdback could be used for the payment of unemployment insurance. I think it is of the utmost importance as a part of the remuneration to which the inmate himself must make a contribution, that there be the payment of unemployment insurance.
I can assure you that one of the biggest problems that this country faces is the fact that the government spends a great deal of money first of all on incarcerating these people because they have broken the laws of society. Then, after we have them in custody we try to rehabilitate them by training so that they will become useful members of society. Then, when their term of imprisonment is up and they are released they come up against the situation which we have had for far too long, namely the serious unemployment situation where the socially responsible unemployed cannot get jobs.
A man coming out of prison is really up against it and what happens? The very few dollars he has are gone. There is no job; there is no unemployment insurance; there is the utmost difficulty in getting welfare. I can assure the Minister of Justice that time after time during this winter, because of my interest in these matters, I have had telephone calls. People have said to me that they were released four weeks ago, six weeks ago, two months ago, and have no jobs and no unemployment insurance and they cannot get welfare. After the first handout from the John
Supply-Labour
Howard Society of British Columbia a person does not get any more as a general rule.
These people ask me, "What am I going to do; what am I expected to do?" I see it personally. The government has spent all this money in trying to rehabilitate these men and these women and it is going right down the drain because they are driven to the point where they say, "I cannot get a job; I have no subsistence; I will try to get away with it again." I think we would be making a far better investment if we were to work out some plan whereby when those people came out, because of their contributions as well as assistance from the government, perhaps not under unemployment insurance itself but in some form along that line that might tie in with it, they could use that money to tide themselves over a difficult time. We would get a better return on the money we spend and there would be a vast number who are now recidivists who would not again commit crimes.
As I say, I can only bring this up under "remuneration" and I most sincerely, from my own personal experience, knowledge and study of this matter, ask the minister to try to work out some plan whereby in desperation those men do not return to crime because they cannot get a job.

I realize that the question I am about to ask is something which may be too involved to answer at this time and that it might be better to deal with it at a later stage, but are there any restrictions placed on the type of books and publications which are available to inmates?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: There is supervision exercised by the warden and chaplain service, yes. As I recall it, I do not think there is any set of regulations in detail laid down on what type of books may be brought in but the warden on the advice to some extent of the chaplain, as I recall it, is responsible for determining whether a book may or may not be brought in.

Item agreed to.
DEPARTMENT OF LABOUR A-Department Special Services-
709. Payments to a province during 1958-59 and 1959-60 fiscal years in accordance with an agreement entered into by the government of Canada and the province, with the approval of the governor in council, that provides for contributions by the government of Canada of amounts not exceeding one half of the cost of labour incurred in the period from the 1st day of December, 1958, to the 30th day of April, 1959, on winter work projects in municipalities as contemplated by the agreement, $15,000,000.
Supply-Labour
Would the minister not like to supply us with a little information before we begin to discuss this item.

Mr. Chairman, the municipal incentive program, to which this item allocates $15 million, resulted from a winter employment conference held in Ottawa in July of last year. Participating in the conference were representatives of provincial and municipal governments, national organizations such as labour organizations, chambers of commerce, the Canadian Manufacturers' Association and many others.
The purpose in calling the conference at that time was to ascertain the views of these people as to how winter unemployment could be best combated. The conference lasted two days and those participating in the conference made a report which, I might say, was made without any direction from the federal government. The result was that suggestions were made as to incentives in order to provide more winter activity.
In October of last year the government also had a conference with representatives of the Canadian federation of mayors and municipalities. The mayors attending the *conference came from large and small communities across the country. During that conference it was suggested by those representing the municipalities that the maximum amount of work, or at least more than in any other way, could be supplied through the efforts of the municipalities on the municipal level. In other words, they felt they could proceed with some of their municipal projects in the winter time provided the additional cost was offset by a contribution from the federal government.
In view of this suggestion the government offered a program to the provinces and through the provinces to the municipalities. This program involved participation by the federal government to the extent of 50 per cent of the total payroll costs in such projects as would not ordinarily be undertaken during the winter. I might say that the plan was accepted enthusiastically by all the provinces and they are participating to quite a large extent in the winter program. The four provinces of Alberta, Saskatchewan, Ontario and Prince Edward Island added an additional incentive by agreeing to pay 25 per cent which meant that municipalities in those provinces would have 75 per cent of the payroll cost borne by the federal and provincial governments. The province of Manitoba offered 30 per cent as their contribution toward the program.
During the first two months the program was in effect, in fact, up to February 6, 1959, 1,395 municipal projects were accepted. They
IMr. Fulton.]
were processed and approved by the provinces and the federal government and most of them are under way at the moment. According to the figures submitted to us by the municipalities in their applications, these 1,395 projects have provided 22,712 additional on-site jobs this winter across Canada. That figure is broken down in this way. In the Atlantic provinces these projects have provided 4,013 jobs, in Quebec 1,763, in Ontario 8,633, in the prairie provinces 6,328, and in British Columbia 1,975, making a total of 22,712.
Projects are still being submitted and processed. There has been no delay. In addition to the on-site jobs, employment has been provided for many more people engaged in the manufacture of materials and supplies and working in other trades and transportation and other services that are involved. It is estimated by those interested in these projects that the figure of 22,712 workers can be tripled in order to arrive at the number who are participating in the program.
The total cost of the projects accepted to date is $57,272,000, of which amount $46,694,000 will be spent during the five months that the program is in effect, that is, from December 1 to April 30. Direct payroll expenditure on projects accepted to date is estimated to be $15,656,000 and the federal share, being 50 per cent, will be approximately $7,751,000.
I am very pleased with the labour content of these projects. For all of the 1,395 projects approved to date the labour content is 38 per cent. We had hoped that it would be close to 30 per cent but it has gone beyond our expectations. I believe this is because the municipalities made a careful survey of projects in order to submit those where the labour content was the highest and I think they should be commended in this respect. It is estimated that the men employed on these projects will work a total of 1,228,358 man days.
Clearly this program has stimulated work and provided jobs during this period of time and will provide jobs in the next two and a half months for this number and I hope many more as projects are submitted for approval. There is no indication at the moment that the municipalities have no more projects to submit because they are coming in at almost the same rate as they did when the plan was announced.
There has been criticism, of course, that the program was late in starting. It is true that the program was not announced until late in October but the fact is that by December 19 over 500 projects had been processed and approved. I do not know whether

there is anything else I can add at the moment except to say that this is a field in which the federal government has never before participated. Its participation is an indication that the government is concerned about unemployment and that we are trying to do something. The program is the result of suggestions made at the conference where industry, labour, the provinces and the municipalities were represented and the result of direct suggestions made by the mayors representing the municipalities at their conference with us in October of last year.

Mr. Chairman, I should like to take part in the discussion of this item because I have a very close acquaintance with the problems confronting the municipalities, the major one, of course, being unemployment. When the government announced the federal-provincial plan to assist municipalities to create employment we in Fort William were very happy about it. Accordingly our municipal council instructed our engineering department to prepare a list of projects which we hoped would come under the scheme, and which included bridges, sewers, roads and parks. These programs would have put several hundred people to work. Accordingly, we sent this list to the department for approval. But, lo and behold, when we received the list back from the department it was so blue-pencilled that the only thing left on the list was the clearing and brushing of park areas and street rights-of-way. Instead of putting hundreds of people to work, as we expected, only 48 men are now actually employed under the scheme.
During the throne speech debate, I made the following observations in connection with this announced program, as recorded on page 88 of Hansard for January 20, 1959:
Having served as mayor of the city of Fort William for eight years, I was delighted to hear that parliament will be asked to assist the municipalities of Canada in financing construction projects. I hope this aid will not be limited to the recently announced winter work program in conjunction with provincial governments. In this connection it may interest you to know that this project has only benefited 120 unemployed in the city of Fort William. I express the hope that the assistance will go beyond the presently prescribed limitations.
I find I was wrongly informed by the municipality, and that the figures were conveyed to me in the hope that the number would reach 120. A few days later, I was informed by letter from the city administrator, and I quote:
For your information, projects involving a total of $73,989.92 were approved by the provincial and federal governments and to date 48 men are being employed clearing and brushing park areas and street right-of-ways. It is likely that they will
Supply-Labour
be employed until April 30, 1959. The work is all straight labour and does not involve the purchase of materials, etc.
I want to assure the Minister of Labour, whom I count as one of my friends, that I do not minimize for one moment the importance of any scheme that will create jobs. We are grateful for any action that will give work to even a few, but I must confess that this program does not begin to meet the seriousness of the unemployment situation in Fort William where, as of January 21, we had 3,010 unemployed, which figure is higher than it was on the same date in 1957.
My views on the matter are more or less embodied in a resolution which I had prepared, but because I might be ruled out of order I am not going to move it at this time. However, I should like to read it:
Whereas, the impact of unemployment falls heavily on municipal governments and
Whereas the present federal-provincial winter work program will not take care of the immediate needs,
Be it resolved that the government give immediate consideration to the extension of the program beyond the present prescribed limitations.
Mr. Chairman, this winter work program, to be really effective, should include construction projects which, because of difficulties in financing, would otherwise be deferred until the municipalities found themselves in a better financial position. I would include new arterial highways bypassing business sections thus relieving traffic in the downtown area; the elimination of railway grade crossings; the widening of arterial highways within city limits; the construction of technical and vocational schools; and the construction of bridges over navigable waters.
The necessity for new bridges in Fort William is real. At the moment there is one bridge connecting the mainland with island No. 2 and a second bridge connecting island No. 2 with island No. 1. Incidentally, these islands are designated by numbers for want of names. We never got around to naming them, but we would be only too happy to do so whenever the government will render additional assistance to enable us to build bridges so that they will not be cut off. If something should happen to the bridge connecting island No. 2, this would have the effect of separating the two islands completely from the mainland. These two islands are suitable for heavy industry and a large industrial development is presently taking place there. On island No. 1 we have the Husky Oil and Refining Company, McColl-Frontenac Oil Co. Ltd., Canada Steamships Lines, Canadian Oil Co. Ltd., and the Canadian Pacific railway. On island No. 2 we have

Supply-Labour
located the British-American Oil Company, K. A. Powell Canada Ltd., Dryden Paper Company, Thunder bay yacht club, Kam boating club, hydro power commission of Ontario, which is now building a $26 million steam generating plant, and the Northern Engineering and Supply Company.
Other firms presently proceeding with large developments include the Canada Cement Company, Huron Chemicals Ltd., and in addition to these two a number of other firms are negotiating with the city for acreage on island No. 2. The size and location of the desired bridges will have to be defined by consulting engineers, but the immediate need is a bridge to provide an alternative to the Canadian Pacific railway bridge presently crossing the Kaministikwia river.
I did not intend to elaborate on the bridge situation in Fort William, but I feel that it provides an illustration which may have parallels in other parts of the country. These are the types of projects which would provide work for a considerable number of men and I therefore urge the government to take another look at the present winter work program and give the municipalities a break which will enable them to undertake worthwhile projects which will be of lasting benefit to the community. In this young, dynamic Canada of ours, there should be no room for widespread unemployment. Leaving all the recriminations of party politics aside, including the statements often made by members on the government side, "What would you do"-well, I offer a proposition here. I offer the suggestion that in addition to an expanded program of assistance to municipalities, assistance to private enterprise to encourage the establishment of new industries in a similar way as is being done in the promotion and stimulation of house construction, would be the answer to one of the major problems confronting Canada today.
You have already heard in this house about the possibility of the closing of the Canada Car plant in the city of Fort William. If that should happen-I am not suggesting it will because I am hoping that the government will soon decide-
Order. I would ask hon. members please to make presentations and suggestions under item 709.

The hon. gentleman was trying to point out that this particular works program in his constituency is inadequate because of a serious layoff. With great respect, Mr. Chairman, I would suggest
fMr. Badanai.]
that he is entitled to mention the circumstances of this layoff in order to point out either the adequacy or the inadequacy of the program.
Carry on. It is a good speech.

On
this matter I should just like to suggest that this is a winter works program and should be dealt with as such. The layoff to which I believe the hon. member is referring is one in a plant in his constituency. I would ask the hon. member to continue.

I am referring to the whole program as an example which would benefit our municipality in the matter of a winter works program. I would just say that if the Canada Car Company fails to receive an order for this vehicle which I have mentioned, if the government had a provision to establish, to finance or to help or assist in financing the establishment of a new industry, I dare say there would be a number of our citizens, including some of those who are presently working at this plant, who would be able and willing to form such a company and with the government's assistance it could be successful and capable of retaining a large skilled labour force employed. If the government persists in belittling or ignoring constructive suggestions such as those I have endeavoured to make, then the members of the government need not feel annoyed if they are reminded by the opposition of the seriousness of the unemployment situation. I submit that the road out of unemployment is not a road paved with platitudes and good intentions. It is a road that can be found only with courage and imagination, as well as the means which the government possesses.
Mr. Chairman-
Would the hon. member permit me to make an observation with respect to what has been said by the hon. member for Fort William?
Yes.

The hon. member for Fort William mentioned that sewers, bridges and other underpasses were not included. It is set out clearly that sewers are included. We have passed a large number of large sewer projects. Bridges are included for the major reconstruction of roads as well as underpasses and culverts. All these things are included.

Yes.

Thank you very much, Mr. Chairman. As I was beginning to say, I wish the unemployed in Canada were as well organized as are other groups in Canada. If that were the case, this item appearing in the estimates at this time would become one of the major subjects for a debate in this house at the current session of parliament. I
Supply[DOT]-Labour
believe it is rather odd that a major item of this kind appears, as it were, after the event and comes before us as one of the items in the supplementary estimates. What I have in mind is this. A matter as important as this item should in my opinion have been presented to the House of Commons at the last session and should have been presented in the form of legislation so that there might have ensued a debate on, first, the need for action along that line and, second, the methods that might be adopted for the successful implementation of that legislation. However, we are obliged to satisfy ourselves now with merely conducting a debate on a matter that appears in the estimates.
I realize that the government at the end of the last session was keenly aware of the fact that a measure of this kind would be necessary in the winter of 1958-59. Unemployment was not receding, as it had so often done, over the summer months or in the course of the summer months and anyone in Canada with any modicum of intelligence at all could foresee the situation that we would be having on our hands in the forthcoming winter. Yet this government would not take parliament into its confidence as to what its plans were.
I am hoping the Minister of Labour is not going to consider that what I have to say is an attack on either himself or the administration of his department. He has certain responsibilities as a minister. However, they are extremely limited. They are limited in the main to administration efforts. However, this item in the estimates involves much more than matters which concern only our Minister of Labour. I feel that when this item in the estimates is being discussed leading members of the government ought to be in their places and ought to be prepared to show how this item meets their commitment to the people of Canada that as long as they are in office no one would suffer because of unemployment. I am going to vote for this program. I am going to vote for this $15 million because I know how necessary it is. Nevertheless it is a pittance. It is a weak program in the light of the need and in the light of the type of program the people of Canada expected this government to produce. After all, Mr. Chairman, this government has now been in office for 20 months, since the election of June 10, 1957, and yet in all of those 20 months we find that their major project to relieve unemployment in Canada consists of their so-called winter works plan that is now before us.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: What about housing?
What about the unemployed?

The minister says, "What about housing?", I am quite prepared to give the

Supply-Labour
minister lull marks on that matter so far as it incidentally relieved to a certain extent the unemployment situation. However, the Minister of Public Works knows full well that housing was coming to a halt in Canada. Private enterprise was deserting the field, and something had to be done. That was the basic reason why the government came forward with its housing program. It was not for the purpose of supplying employment. It just happened to suit the argument of the government of Canada. If the minister remembers what I warned him about last year, I said he would find that as rapidly as he poured money into housing, private enterprise would leave the housing field and devote its funds to more lucrative enterprises in Canada, such as gas pipe lines and the like. However, I do realize that we are getting a little off the estimate now before us. This is the one major item which has been presented by this government to solve the question of unemployment in Canada. This sum of $15 million even by itself, when looked at in money terms, will do very little indeed to restore prosperity and confidence in the economic and business field.
I would like to say a few words on the statement given to us by the Minister of Labour. I appreciate that the minister and his department are not responsible. They are given the unpleasant task of making the best show of a very badly conceived enterprise in the first place. The minister said that this estimate appears before us partly as a result of the report of the conference on winter unemployment. I was in Ottawa at the time this conference was held. I believe almost all of us were in Ottawa; at any rate, we were supposed to be here at that time. Parliament was sitting at the time, yet after the conference we repeatedly asked the minister whether he could advise us whether any action might be forthcoming as a result of the recommendations emanating from this conference. I applaud the calling of the conference but, however, parliament was left to go home on September 6 without being offered any concrete proposals which had emanated from the conference for our consideration.
The minister also indicated that this program may possibly be the result of the conference that the Prime Minister held with the Canadian federation of mayors and municipalities. I believe the minister there engaged in some really wishful thinking, because if my observations of that meeting of the mayors and municipalities are correct, first of all it took place on October 6 and 7 of last year, which is well on into the winter
[Mr. Regier.l
in many parts of Canada. The wire that the Prime Minister sent to the premiers of the provinces or to the provincial governments was not sent until October 27, which was fully three weeks later. However, be that as it may, at the conference of October 6 and 7 to which the minister referred the mayors and reeves of municipalities were told, in effect, to go home and look at their assessment rolls to see whether assessments could not be raised a bit. They were told to look at their tax rate and see whether the mill rate could not be raised a little bit, and if they had any difficulty in borrowing money for major municipal works projects, perhaps it was because they were not offering a high enough rate of interest on the market to attract investors.
Mr. Chairman, I cannot agree that this was as a result of the report of the conference on winter unemployment, because if it had been, parliament, which was meeting at the time, had the right to expect the government to make some announcement to parliament-

Mr. Chairman on a question of privilege, the hon. member is questioning my statement that this matter was not discussed with the mayors and as a result this plan was put into effect. I wish to inform the hon. member that he will have to take my word for it: I was present and discussed it with them.

I thank the minister for his interruption, and I am very sorry if I created a wrong impression in his mind. However, I do not believe that I said that this project was not discussed. I only doubted that it really emanated as a result of those discussions, because it took three full weeks after that meeting until the provincial governments were advised. Major projects like this, cannot be undertaken by municipalities on almost no notice whatsoever. I cannot think of any major project requiring employment in my municipality of Burnaby or Port Moody which can be undertaken without first having to prepare plans and to submit those plans by way of money by-laws to the rate payers. Then after that they have to go to the money markets and sell their bonds and their debentures. I notice that it was not until some time after October 26 that the municipalities actually received the details, which made it useless for the purpose of providing employment.

He said: Mr. Speaker, it is indeed a great honour for me to sponsor this bill on behalf of the Canadian Medical Association. This association was founded in Quebec in 1867 and was incorporated by act of federal parliament in 1909. The first president of the association was Sir Charles Tupper.
The association represents 80 to 85 per cent of the practising members of the medical profession in Canada. Throughout the years it has done everything possible to promote the health and well-being of Canadian citizens. As all hon. members are aware the practice and scope of medicine and its impact upon our citizens have changed tremendously since 1909. The purpose of this bill is simply to modernize the constitution of the association and bring it up to date. It seeks to repeal sections 2 and 7 of chapter 62 of the statutes of 1909. The important additions provided by this bill are contained in paragraphs (f) and (g) of clause 2 of the present bill which reads as follows:
2. (f) to promote the interests of the members of the association and to act on their behalf in the promotion thereof;
(g) to grant sums of money out of the funds of the association for the furtherance of these projects;
In January of 1957 provisions came into effect to set up a pension and retirement scheme on a voluntary basis for members of the association. These changes were made possible because of provisions in the Income Tax Act introduced in that year. The alterations in the constitution of the association are required so that the Canadian Medical Association can look after its members. The other changes are related to the wider fields that are now within the realm of the members of the association. Some examples of these, of course, are the fields of industrial medicine, public health and cancer control.
The changes in section 7 merely represent a request to remove the limitations presently imposed on the value of real estate which the association may own. Mr. Speaker, I should like to say a few words in support of this bill. As the hon. gentleman who has just taken his seat has said, this association is one with a long and creditable history of public service, the first president being a former distinguished member of the Canadian parliament, Sir Charles Tupper, who at one time was prime minister of Canada and who was an outstanding physician.
And a distinguished Nova Scotian.

As the hon. gentleman has just said, Sir Charles Tupper came from Nova Scotia. He was not the only person from Nova Scotia to have made a contribution to the Canadian Medical Association but he will long be remembered for the outstanding contributions he has made.
As one who was minister of national health and welfare of this country for some years I feel I may speak with some authority about the contribution which the Canadian Medical Association makes to the profession of medicine and generally to the work of improving the health services of our country. I have in mind particularly men like Dr. Clarence Routley who, as secretary of this association for such a long time and as president of the association at a time when he was also president of a much wider body comprised of physicians of the commonwealth and other countries as well, has won the gratitude of the Canadian Medical Association, the people of Canada and the government of Canada. His leadership and co-operation in the association during the time I served as minister of national health and welfare deserve profound gratitude. He represented Canada as indeed have other officers of this association at meetings of the World Health Organization on several occasions.
The present vice-president of the association, Dr. Kirk Lyon, who would be president but for the fact that His Royal Highness the Duke of Edinburgh occupies that post at the present time, is also a man who has made a great contribution both to the Ontario Medical Association and to the Canadian Medical Association. I am very pleased about the services that Dr. Lyon has made because he comes from my own county of Essex. Dr. Murray Douglas the president of the-Ontario Medical Association also comes frorr

this county and both these distinguished gentlemen have made extremely worthwhile contributions.
At a time when there was much criticism of the proposal for hospital insurance introduced and placed on the statute books by the previous administration the Canadian Medical Association gave its support to the proposal and through such personalities as Dr. Routley greatly facilitated the public understanding of a measure that is now widely accepted in most parts of Canada.

The house resumed from Friday, February 8, consideration of the motion of Mr. Weichel for the second reading of Bill S-4, to incorporate the Waterloo Mutual Insurance Company.

Mr. Speaker, the purpose of the bill now before us is to change the basis of the charter of the Waterloo Mutual Insurance Company From a provincial charter to a federal charter; in other words, to bring it under the jurisdiction of the federal superintendent of insurance.
The Waterloo Mutual Fire Insurance Company, which is referred to as a provincial company, was incorporated under the provincial laws of Ontario in 1863. As one of the early incorporated mutual insurance companies of Ontario it has been doing business for about 96 years and now seeks federal incorporation to place itself in a position to benefit from the good will created by its past performance. Under the act of incorporation the new company will continue the business of the former company and assume its assets and liabilities.
The Waterloo Mutual is the last of the mutual companies which were formed years ago in Ontario such as the Gore District Mutual, the Perth Mutual and the Economical Mutual, all of which have obtained federal incorporations and are now operating on the basis of federal charters. This Waterloo company seeks to join those which are now

operating as dominion companies. Dominion registration facilitates the extension of its business beyond Ontario. Fire, automobile and other casualty business in Ontario is limited. This company would like to extend its activities to the other provinces of the dominion. Also, in this country about 80 per cent of the life insurance business is in the hands of Canadian insurance companies; whereas casualty, fire and other casualty insurance is in the hands of Canadian companies only to the extent of about 20 per cent. The remainder is in the hands of British, United States and foreign-owned insurance companies. Therefore, the premium income is diverted out of this country to other foreign countries.
The number of life insurance companies in the United States and Canada which are placing mortgages on real estate insist that the fire insurance policies on this real estate must be policies issued by dominion incorporated companies and this Waterloo company finds that it is losing quite a number of its better risks, and naturally they would like to retain them.
Another reason is that when they come to seek reinsurance with the other dominion incorporated companies the provincial companies are treated as more or less unlicensed re-insurers by the dominion department of insurance and they have to deposit insurance to cover their insurance risk with a chartered trust company, which is an inconvenience and an added expense to the provincial companies. Also, the federal insurance companies come under the inspection of the dominion insurance laws, which are a great deal stricter than the provincial laws.
I believe this, in a general way, pretty well covers the reasons for this bill which contains all the provisions required to protect the policy holders as well as the public.
In the event that this incorporation goes through, I may say that there is no intention to change the board of directors or the shareholders or to interfere in any way whatsoever with the capital stock of the company. This bill has the support and the recommendation of the superintendent of insurance who piloted it through the other place and recommended its passage.

Mr. Speaker, may I make one brief comment in support of this bill? With respect to the action of the company in increasing its jurisdiction and its ability to compete in the field of insurance I should like to make this comment. I agree with the remarks made here by the sponsor and I believe in the other place. The excuse given that certain

mortgage and insurance companies today insist and require that they place insurance elsewhere rather than with this provincial company is an excuse which was put forward by some of those companies without legal or ethical right in order to give certain advantages to a preferred group of insurance companies. I hope that this company will not be disappointed in increasing its jurisdiction or status by becoming a dominion company by finding that perhaps some other excuses have been given by some of those other companies. I feel at times that some of the mortgage and insurance companies change the insurance, although the mortgage says only that the property should be insured up to the value of the mortgage.
I also note that the applicants are of Canadian origin and seem to be in the constituency of the sponsors of the bill. I was wondering whether the shareholders come primarily from the province of Ontario or the area of the sponsors. I would also like to know whether the sponsor is going to have representatives of the company present when it goes to the committee?

Mr. Speaker, when the house was giving consideration last Friday to private members' bills we had an interesting debate on the practice of divorce in the Canadian parliament. A number of interesting contributions were made in that debate. I think every speaker had some new thought to offer on this subject. Perhaps at this time I can make a few comments on some of the more important points that were made. The hon. member for Saskatoon (Mr. Jones) raised two questions that I think should be answered. As you and the house will recall, Mr. Speaker, I said then that as the sponsor of the bills I would not move bills in the house when there was lobbying in support of the bills outside of the House of Commons but inside the parliament buildings. I felt that this was a good stand to take for the protection of members of parliament who frequently, at the request of their constituents, have to do something to help in divorce cases. Judging from the reaction to this statement, I can only conclude that it was a very happy and fortuitous one because I have heard of no disagreement. However, one hon. member did point out that there might be a danger that the person on the losing side of the case would do some lobbying and if I then refused to move the bill the person in the wrong would have achieved a miscarriage of justice and the person in the right would not obtain the divorce. There is certainly no intention of that happening. I am glad the hon. member did point out that possibility.

Private Bills
This policy, of course, would only be used to thwart attempts by people to put undue pressure on members of parliament. Certainly it would not be a policy designed to help the guilty.
In the course of my remarks I dealt somewhat with the hotel and motel cases and the law that pertains to the decisions in the provincial courts on the balance of probability. I said that whereas it has been assumed for a long time that if two people were found under suspicious circumstances in a hotel or motel it could be inferred they had gone there for the purpose of committing adultery it might now appear that they had gone for the purpose of acquiring evidence for a divorce. I merely raised the point to indicate the great reliance on the hotel and motel type of evidence that is prevalent all across Canada today. I certainly did not want to indicate that there was any such inference drawn in the provincial courts. However, it would be useful to point out that parliament, in dealing with divorce, does not act upon whimsy, upon whether it likes the colour of one person's eyes or dislikes the colour of another person's eyes.
It is true that we do have the power to be whimsical in our decisions if we so choose. However, it has been the practice for years, in the other place and in the House of Commons, to determine these cases upon legal principles and to follow the reasoning that is applied in courts of justice. In that way we give citizens who come here petitioning for relief no more rights than they would have if they had gone to provincial courts. On the other hand, we give them no less rights.
It has been the practice in our committee, for example, to have the services of Dr. Maurice Ollivier and Mr. Eobert J. Batt. They are in attendance at our meetings so that we may be properly instructed on the law whenever the need for instruction arises. I made my point that the law could sometimes take a different view of what went on in hotels and motels not to indicate that any such inferences were now being made from these hotel and motel cases. However, at some future time some court might very well consider the whole matter, and consider modern times and modern trends as compared to what went on 100 years ago, and might lay down some judicial principle that hotel and motel evidence could not be regarded as qualifying for the granting of a divorce. That day has not come but I believe that some day a court will have to encounter it. If the law is changed in that regard, then I would point out that we will be so advised, both here and in the other
[Mr. McCleave.l
place, and we will have to act accordingly. We shall be guided by any new legal principles that come along.
The hon. member for Timiskaming (Mr. Peters) and the hon. member for Davenport (Mr. Morton) made strong pleas to get these cases out of parliament and out of the House of Commons. I make only a very brief comment on that. Under the British North America Act divorce jurisdiction became a matter for parliament, something that the fathers of confederation conceived in their wisdom. Over the years arrangements have been made so that in eight provinces these cases are heard in the courts, but this is not so in the province of Quebec or the province of Newfoundland. I think the people who make suggestions about removing divorce jurisdiction from parliament in these two cases are perhaps blinding themselves to reality.
We are dealing with matters belonging to two particular provinces. If we had before us suggestions from members of those particular provinces that they would like the cases so removed, perhaps we would be farther along the road to the day when parliament would not have to deal with divorce. It seems to me that to make these suggestions now is rather dangerous. I know that as a member from Nova Scotia I would be rather wrathy if someone from British Columbia were to come along and suggest how we should run affairs in Nova Scotia. I am sure the same reasoning would apply to a gentleman from one of these provinces if such suggestions were made by someone from another province. I think that this matter of parliament divesting itself from divorce jurisdiction, if it is ever to be dealt with properly, the suggestion and initiative for that sort of action must come from the responsible people in the two provinces concerned.
Several of the speakers in the debate last week, Mr. Speaker, mentioned some of the problems in connection with the work of the committee itself. I do not intend to deal with them before the house. There will be changes suggested in the committee and hon. members will have an opportunity there to discuss them.
There is one final point. One of the speakers last week made a suggestion that contentious divorce cases were being decided last session along party lines in the House of Commons when they came to a vote. As I recall those two cases, that was certainly not what happened. Except for the two members of the C.C.F. who tended to stick closely together on one side of the case or another,

the members of other parties were split in opinion as between one side of the case or the other.
Motion agreed to.

Mr. Speaker, with respect to Bill No. SD-19, there are certain elements that appear in the evidence which I think should be considered by the house. I might say first of all that I have no objection whatsoever to the applicant in this case being successful in her 66968-9-65i

petition for a divorce. The evidence, particularly that with regard to the treatment of the child, leads one to believe that she should have had a divorce long ago. I have here the evidence taken before the divorce committee of the other place, and it would appear that the applicant applied for and received a separation order from the superior court of Quebec in the spring of 1954. That order made it mandatory that she be paid the sum of $25 a month for the support of the child. This money was paid for almost one year and then no further payments were made. The applicant did not press for further payments, being content to look after the child with the money that she herself earned as a saleslady. The startling point in the evidence is to be found halfway down page 12 where I find the following:
Q. I understand your daughter is at school, is that correct?
A. Yes.
Q. Has he-
Meaning the husband
-ever made any inquiries about his daughter at all?
A. Nothing at all.
In other words, for three years he has paid nothing for the support of the child and has made no attempt to maintain any normal contact with the child whatsoever. However, in spite of these circumstances and the background of the case it is still true that when you read the evidence you see that it is strictly circumstantial. As I am not a lawyer like the chairman of the private bills committee, the taller member from Halifax, I am not sufficiently versed in the law to know whether the circumstantial evidence offered is good or not good. Having read it myself, I consider it to be satisfactory but nevertheless it is still circumstantial evidence.
This case has one advantage. Instead of being the stereotyped motel or hotel type of case such as come before the unfortunate members of the private bills committee in great numbers, this case happens to have authenticity and a ring of truth about it because the events took place in the gentleman's apartment. I listened to the hon. member for Halifax (Mr. McCleave) when he spoke a few days ago on the occasion of the first series of divorce bills coming before the house. He said then that he thought that the people of Newfoundland and Quebec would resent any change in the present method of handling these cases. I wonder whether that is quite true. After all, divorces are being granted to residents of Newfoundland and Quebec. It is a fact. These divorce cases come here, are reviewed very thoroughly in the other place, are given as much consideration as we can

Private Bills
possibly give them and are processed rather quickly considering the amount of work involved, but this is still not the right way to deal with the matter.
The two provinces concerned have said that parliament should handle this type of business because they do not want anything to do with it. However, since other provinces have established a procedure for the handling of divorce cases, is it not within the power of parliament to set up a special divorce court?
