Mr. Speaker, I rise at this time to make a few comments on this particular divorce bill. The unfortunate aspect of divorce bills is perhaps the suffering involved, the sympathy that goes to the individuals concerned and the fact that in having to come before parliament as they do they are engaged in a sort of parliamentary Russian roulette in the sense that when petitioning for a divorce these people never know which particular bill is going to be picked on by members of parliament.
I have occasion to disagree with the hon. member for Halifax (Mr. McCleave) in a sense when he said that only the members from Newfoundland and Quebec were interested in divorce matters before parliament. I feel that this is a matter of interest to all members of parliament because it is the entire

parliamentary time that is being taken up and not just that of the provinces of Newfoundland and Quebec.
As the particular divorce before us, the facts indicate that the petitioner was married on November 5, 1940, separated from her husband in September, 1953, and there was a separation judgment in the spring of 1954. I think perhaps the most justifiable item in all the evidence dealing with the divorce is succinctly expressed in the statement found at page 12. It was a question by Senator Barbour to the petitioner which went as follows:
Q. Would you take your husband back now?
A. No, I wouldn't.
In reviewing the evidence contained in this report I think that is perhaps the most valid grounds for granting the divorce. The hon. member for Vancouver South who preceded me said he did not wish to speak on the matter of the evidence. However, I feel that that is a matter of a great deal of importance since, as the hon. member for Halifax pointed out to us, we in parliament are sitting in a sense in a judicial capacity and all we have before us in most instances is the evidence presented by the Senate. From that we go through a feat of logic and try to ascertain whether or not we would be justified logically, and perhaps morally, in granting the specific divorce.
In the present situation, the investigation went on over a period from July 4, 1958, to September 14, 1958. The only relevant dates seem to be September 12, which was a Friday, and September 13 and September 14 which, of course, were Saturday and Sunday consecutively. The first investigator said that he had received a call, I believe it was, about two o'clock in the morning-this is on the morning of September 12-from his coinvestigator to the effect that there was somebody in the respondent's apartment. The evidence stated that a woman had been seen in Mr. Dobie's apartment since late in the evening and it seemed that she was still there. He had not seen her leave. That is the first evidence that we had as to the woman named being in the particular apartment. They renewed their vigilance on Saturday, September 13, at nine o'clock in the morning and apparently the only evidence there was that they saw the lady go into a supermarket, returning with some groceries and then go into the apartment.
One of the difficulties in the feat of logic that we are asked to perform in the present case is that it is not indicated as to how many entrances there are to the apartment. Only one entrance is mentioned and apparently the apartment is located on the ground floor. It also apparently goes into some two

or three other apartments. But the vigilant private investigators have not mentioned in the evidence whether or not there was a back door and whether the woman named might have been leaving and coming in by another exit. They spent apparently most of Saturday carefully watching the apartment and they stayed watching it until 2.15 a.m. in the morning. Then one of the investigators apparently at 2.15 in the morning, decided that there was no point in remaining further, that there would be no further developments. Apparently this shrewd investigator decided -evidently it was an apartment where I imagine the blinds are pulled

that eight o'clock in the morning was perhaps the time to come back. But then on Saturday, apparently being rather early risers, the first and second investigator met at 8.05 in the morning and in the words of the evidence of one investigator:
After discussing the situation we decided to risk a contact, so we knocked on the door of Mr. Dobie's basement apartment. At first there was no response. We could hear somebody moving around very quietly inside, and I called through the door and asked for Mr. Dobie, and a minute or two later he came and said, "Who is it?"-
And so on. So from the time there was a knock on the door there was an interval, according to the investigators, of one or two minutes. Then the investigators, being rather ingenious individuals, managed to think of an excuse to get into the bedroom to make a telephone call and, arriving in the bedroom, of course found the lady in bed. It was a double bed and she was apparently alone at the time. The interesting thing about the evidence which I think would be fairly important is that the investigator said:
From what we could see she didn't seem to have any clothes on at all.
Although it is stated that she had a blanket surrounding her. They went on to mention that there were several articles of underclothing distributed around the room and that there was a pair of trousers on the dresser. But from the evidence presented, I am unable to ascertain whether Mr. Dobie answered the door without his trousers or whether in fact he had a suit with two pairs of pants. The investigator never thought to clarify the situation as to Mr. Dobie's apparent state of dress or undress. If the circumstances of adultery are as alleged, then Mr. Dobie must have dressed very quickly from the time they knocked in order to arrive at the door in a habitable state. This, Mr. Chairman, is the only indication and the only evidence that we have that there was adultery. There was a knock on the door. The gentleman answered very promptly.

There was a lady in the other room in bed who may or may not have been undressed. This is presented to us on the basis, of course, that there was adultery involved.
I worry a great deal about our responsibility because in a sense we are a judicial body. If I may, I should like to turn briefly to what the legal situation is on the evidence of adultery. I should like first of all to refer to the "Canadian Encyclopedic Digest", the Ontario edition, at page 194, where we find the following:
Even though the charges of adultery are not denied they must be proved to the satisfaction of the court. The burden of establishing adultery always rests on petitioner.
Then Power, in his excellent book on divorce, disagrees to a slight extent on the onus of proof required as suggested by the hon. member for Halifax. It is with respect that I quote this authority. Power, in "The Law of Divorce in Canada", at page 310 states as follows:
Even though the charges of adultery are not denied they must be proved to the satisfaction of the court.
Then there is a quotation from the judgment in the case of Sandler v. Sandler, Davies and Johnstone (1934), Probate 149. This is by Sir Boyd Merriman:
In matrimonial causes there is a third party who is even more vitally concerned, perhaps, than the two parties themselves, the state. It is regarded as a matter of public importance that the marriage tie should be maintained and that dissolution of the marriage should only be decreed on grounds allowed by the law.
Then in Russell v. Russell (1924) Appeal Cases 687, Lord Summer states as follows:
They-
That is the judges.
-watch the admissibility of the evidence tendered in undefended divorce cases as vigilantly as if they were protecting the interests of a prisoner undefended by counsel.
Perhaps on the point I referred to as to the burden of proof I may refer to the "Canadian Encyclopedic Digest" at page 196:
The standard of proof in Ontario is not that imposed on the crown in a criminal prosecution, but Is the standard required in a civil action only. The judicial mind must be "satisfied" that the act of adultery was in fact committed, but it need not be satisfied to the extent of a moral certainty as in a criminal case. Evidence that creates only suspicion, surmise or conjecture is of course insufficient. It is necessary that the quality and quantity of the evidence be such as to lead the tribunal, whether judge or jury, acting with care and caution, to the fair and reasonable conclusion that the act was committed.
Reference was made on the same page to a case where the plaintiff's husband deliberately brought a strange woman into the house and got her to undress and get into bed with

Private Bills
him at a time and place when they were sure to be discovered by the plaintiff, and it was held that the inference that adultery had been committed was so weak and improbable that it could not be found as a fact to have been committed. In those circumstances we have both people in bed together at the same time.
May I refer again to page 197 to another case where the court did not infer adultery from the mere fact that the respondent wife, who had separated from her husband, visited the co-respondent several times at his home to do washing and cooking for him, and occasionally stayed overnight, which is a case somewhat parallel with the one before us.
One of the most important aspects is the question of the professional investigator, which is the only evidence before us here. Again in the "Canadian Encyclopedic Digest" at page 198 it is stated:
The evidence of a professional investigator, who is engaged in the business of seeking out acts of misconduct on the part of persons against whom it is desired to institute action for divorce, if uncorroborated by evidence other than that of his own employee, will be scrutinized very carefully; and where such evidence is not conclusive of adultery, but at best shows imprudent conduct on the part of those implicated and an opportunity to commit a matrimonial offence, the action will be dismissed.
So I feel that on the basis of the evidence that we have before us as parliamentarians, if we were acting as judges in the instant case, we would not grant the divorce. I feel, with the difficulties of the case before us, it would be sufficient for us, as parliamentarians, to grant the divorce on the mere fact that the parties are separated and obviously cannot get along together, without going through the rather unusual manoeuvres, shall we say, to obtain the evidence necessary to try and satisfy parliament. I feel, it is indicative of the fact, as mentioned by the hon. member for Vancouver South (Mr. Broome), that either we should stop having divorces from Quebec or Newfoundland, or in the alternative there should be a separate court which will be in the position adequately to investigate and ascertain that the divorces were granted. Because, as 1 mentioned earlier, there is an obligation not only to the individuals concerned but also to the state to see that justice is done.
